#3905. Atmosfar is a giddy aerial exploration game after the heart of No Man's Sky, but I'm already trying to escape it

Oh hi there! Why yes, I am free to chat. Please excuse the wind noise, I'm currently tumbling to my doom in Atmosfar, after getting lost in a cloud bank and exhausting my fuel. This kind of thing happens to me regularly in Atmosfar - an open world survival game that plays out across clusters of floating islands, with players scooting about in adorable, propellor-powered airships.

Many of the islands are quite large, with proper landing pads and bases set up by NPC scavengers. Many of them teem with non-human life: rainforests full of nectar droplets and carnivorous plants, meadows of ponderous honking lizards, and mossy grottos where you'll find caches of batteries and possibly get eaten by mantids. It's important to make the most of these larger islands, gathering materials for crafting at your deployable campsite (which straps pleasingly to the back of your whirring fly-mobile). It's particularly important to mine hydrogen crystals you can refine into fuel.

None of that's for me, though! I am a true spirit of the sky. The only fuel I need is my imagination. The only objective marker I acknowledge is the omnidirectional Call to Adventure. Besides, when you do run out of fuel in Atmosfar, you're actually unlocking two exciting minigames. The first consists of leaping from the cockpit and vainly trying to jetpack to the nearest walkable surface. The second consists of racing to overtake your plummeting airship and re-enter the cockpit before you smash into any islands beneath. I'm playing that second minigame right now. Come to papa, my beautiful turboprop son! Ah, balls.

Atmosfar is out in Steam early access today, with plans to stay in early access for at least nine months. I think it has some juice, though I am admittedly already trying to play it against the grain - and at times, trying to do things its technology doesn't quite allow.

It casts you as an interplanetary pioneer who, due to some minor infraction, has been locked up in a factory: a dreary opening area with some corpo-satire elements, from which you are soon liberated by an electrical storm. Busting past the sentry drones, you scramble down a cliffside and discover your very first Wasp hovercar. From there, you have more or less free rein of the game's opening biome, though there's a critical path of tutorials and NPC encounters you'll want to follow for the sake of unlocks, like the jetpack.

The scattered islands do a fair job of luring you from your HUD objectives (the HUD itself is a bit murky, in any case – I struggled to make connections between waypoints and quests in my journal). Even if there's nothing to capital-i Interact with, it's a pleasure to alight on some drifting gobbet of soil and flowers, peer into the crevices, and maybe take a few photos of distant astral mountains.

The searing emptiness all around makes the design of each island feel more precise and careful, gift-wrapped for the player. I find that I'm most interested in the tinier islands, the ones that were presumably a secondary consideration for developers Apog Labs, and maybe handed off to a junior staffer. I gaze at a random grass tuft and try to guess how much ingenuity went into the placement of something many pilots will totally ignore.

I'm already chafing against the survival systems a bit, however. Based on a couple of hours of cloudsteading, Atmosfar's core ingredients aren't particularly novel or involving. There's no tree-chopping, thank god, but you will spend many moments pointing your extractor at a nugget of glowing resourcegook, splitting it into plastic sheets and steel girders and so forth.

Many of the opening missions involve toing and froing between deposits and your airship or camp. It's humdrum stuff. The game's non-player scavengers seem like quest-givers first, characters second. Your inventory size is limited, to begin with. Deeper in, there's the opportunity to construct a huge airbase, the Cloud Cruiser, which I'm really hoping doesn't need refuelling. Although it would be a great joke to accidentally drop one with several co-op buds inside.

I've spent most of my two hours in Atmosfar in headlong retreat from the tutorial quests, trying to reach places I sense I'm not supposed to, without paying my dues to the crafting system. This includes both the ruddier, volcanic areas higher up, which I do believe I can reach, if I bother to refine enough fuel. But I'm more captivated, right now, by what lies beneath.

During a nighttime mission to gather eggs for some outpost chef, I gave into curiosity and aimed my Wasp straight down, spiralling past lonely stalactites with no creature population, into a swirling turquoise abyss full of bare, indistinct rock. As I descended, the game's tech began to creak and fizzle, as though strained by increasing gravity. My ride's exhaust condensed and flattened into glitchy flakes.

I ignored the simulation's protests, holding my course like Ahab aiming a harpoon at Moby Dick's kisser, till a "leaving mission area" reset timer yanked me up short. I ascended to just above the cut-off point, and gawped at the horizon. A juddering white ring enclosed the world, surrounded by wrinkled LIDAR pulses that made me think of thoughts coursing through brain tissue.

Now, this was an adventure. I flapped around a bit, battling turbulence, and managed to land on one of the weirdly unadorned, formless boulders. Who made this? Some procedural generation system, or did somebody actually have to 'hand-craft' these places that are probably not for serious human inquiry or habitation? I shot a few flares over the side and tried to deploy my campsite, but there was too little space on the boulder. Then the sun rose, slowly staining the milky blue fastness pink, and revealing the crisper silhouettes of the properly designed and navigable islands high above.

That last screenshot is my favourite so far - the rosy, rugged beauty of Atmosfar and the bizarre quirks of its technology reaching a strangely persuasive accord. There's only one issue: I've run out of fuel again. I guess I could yeet myself into the void and reset to the nearest landing pad, but that doesn't feel like something a true Spirit of the Sky would do. I guess I'll have to enlist another RPS scribe as a co-op partner and have them come fetch me. Perhaps they can complete the tutorials first and rock up in one of those Cloud Cruiser things. In the meantime, you can get your fill of Atmosfaring via Steam.

'Tis the season, spooky season, and I am also one of PCG's RPG guys. Thus, scary RPGs to celebrate the Halloween spirit must be organized and expounded upon. In a genre that often delivers numbers-based power fantasies in no particular rush, it can be difficult to elicit fear from the player. So when that does happen, I am listening, learning, and taking notes.

I've organized the entries in escalating order of scariness, culminating in a game I want to try some day, but freaks me the hell out just by reputation alone.

This article is brought to you by No More Room in Hell 2.

Kotor 2 is one of my favorite games, and it delivers this overall grim, grimy, hopeless atmosphere like nothing else in Star Wars. Many RPGs consolidate their horror into one or two super-freaky parts, and The Sith Lords boasts a few memorable set pieces in this regard.

The academy on Korriban is particularly affecting for me: This ruined, haunted school where untold suffering took place in the relatively recent past. Seeing it in its gruesome prime in Kotor 1 only adds to the effect. You've seen what the beast can do, and now you're poking its corpse.

Shout out as well to the opening bit on Peragus, specifically the part where ghost ship Harbinger docks with the station. The whole sequence is a very fun and loving riff on System Shock, and I'll always remember this gnarly audio log that introduces one of the game's main antagonists.

Fallout is a series that has reinvented itself over and over again, but no other entry has quite matched the sense of desolation in the 1997 original. Even the most gore-slick, in-your-face edgy portions of Fallout 3 don't quite do it for me in the same way.

More than anything, I just think of the ethering, "nothing is scarier" sight of the Vault Dweller standing alone amid tiles of empty desert, the drone of Mark Morgan's ominous soundtrack your only company⁠—assuming you're not just left in utter silence.

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

The incongruity of jolly old radio bops used to be a far smaller portion of the Fallout soundscape, with the music more dominated by stuff like "Vat of Goo" and "City of Lost Angels." As far as the visual experience goes, the yawning crater of The Glow remains one of the most quietly disturbing images I've ever seen in a game.

That's to say nothing of The Master. New Vegas' lineup of morally questionable faction leaders are some all-time great videogame antagonists, but they're not as unnerving as The Master. This twisted, gestalt creature gives me pause no matter how many times I two-shot it with a Turbo Plasma Rifle (or talk it into killing itself), and the simultaneous tragedy and inhumanity of its vision creeps me the hell out. And that unique FEV mummy death screen? Fuhgeddaboudit.

Lunacid's lonely, forgotten world calls to mind FromSoftware's best, but it's somehow even more cryptic and offputting than the work of that legendarily cryptic, offputting studio. There are plenty of particularly scary levels, for a start: The Accursed Tomb is an early winner, a pitch-dark labyrinth inhabited by faceless zombies, the top halves of their heads removed in a voluntary procedure meant to deliver enlightenment.

But the real freak shit lives in The Mausoleum, a semi-hidden zone patrolled by Death itself. The Grim Reaper will spawn and chase you down whenever you enter this area, lending a frantic urgency to any exploration. Things only get worse if you craft a turbo-hidden sword to kill this otherwise-unkillable foe.

Killing Death messes up your game. In exchange for its powerful scythe, nearly all friendly NPCs disappear, and you'll constantly be chased down by spectre enemies unique to this mode. The Death state can be reversed, but only with a ton of grinding.

This hidden mode, which always reminded me of the evil playthrough of Undertale or Nighttime Anor Londo in Dark Souls, is one of Lunacid's deepest layers of creepy weirdness. But the game is full of stuff like it, a constant process of uncovering new icebergs of lore and mechanics that made me feel like I never fully grasped what was going on.

Skald is one of my favorite RPGs of the decade, maybe all time at this point, and it works on so many levels. As former PCG editor Robin Valentine pointed out in his 2024 preview, there is nothing else like Skald's combo of high fantasy (not quite low fantasy, mid fantasy? That sounds like I'm saying it's "mid") with cosmic horror.

You play as a group of outsiders stumbling onto a Class 5 Cthulhu situation, and while it calls to mind Bloodborne with its portrayal of an outer god-worshipping society, things weren't always like this. Skald provides context, reminders of a world that hasn't gone mad, to elevate the sheer what the hell you're witnessing in the Outer Isles.

It's insane that a game with pixel art graphics can evoke so much dread, and Skald hits you with moments of cosmic revelation that crescendo in one of the most bonkers endings I've ever seen in an RPG, the sheer outer darkness of it all underscored by the lengths Skald goes to make you care about its world and characters. Demon King is more stressful and unpleasant moment-to-moment, but the contrasts of Skald, the rollercoaster ride of its story, owe a lot to how much of a classic-style CRPG it is.

Demon King is a really scary game with RPG elements, while Skald is all the more memorable and horrifying because it is an RPG. And that's why it gets the crown for me.

Taking inspiration primarily from Berserk in the first game, Fear & Hunger is an unforgiving voyage to a dark, dark place, one where shocking sexual violence, mutilation, and utter negation of dignity and humanity are explored in lurid detail. There is no compromise with good taste. The fact that these games are allowed on Steam and not the far more tame Horses is just one of those funny things! I'd like both to be there, to be clear.

Fear & Hunger's low-fi JRPG graphics and anime-esque art create the slightest distance from its horrors. The games also, I think, justify their dizzying level of transgressiveness with nuanced storytelling and a uniquely hopeless fantasy world. Fear & Hunger is one of my favorite examples to point to for the value of transgressive art, particularly as it pertains to games.

I'm fascinated by this series. I've read about it, watched let's plays, and spoiled much of the plot. I'd still like to play both games some day⁠—I own them on Steam⁠—but the thought of immersing myself in so much misery and degradation for the duration of a full RPG, let alone two, makes me physically queasy. I'll get around to it eventually.

The Dunwich Building and Dunwich Borers, respectively. Both twist Bethesda's engine until it screams to make shock flashbacks to before the Great War work, and I just love the deep pool of water with the freaky eye at the bottom in Borers. Stumbling onto these bad boys late at night for the first time, not knowing what to expect? That's Bethesda's capacity to surprise and delight at its best. The rest of these games just aren't that scary⁠, but these moments deserve a shout.

#3903. Capcom's golden streak continues as Onimusha and Pragmata sell well, but Monster Hunter Wilds conspicuously absent from financial report

Capcom has revealed updated sales figures for its new and successful games, including Onimusha: Way of the Sword, Pragmata, and Resident Evil Requiem. But for some reason, Monster Hunter Wilds is absent from the report.

Capcom's half-year report, for the period running 1st April to 30th September, saw growth in both revenue and profit across nearly all segments of the business. In games, much of that was driven by digital sales, which continue to account for the vast majority of the publisher's income.

The first half of FY2026 was especially strong for Capcom owing to the release of multiple critically acclaimed and financially successful titles. Onimusha: Way of the Sword has now sold over 1.7m copies, up from the 1m it sold at launch. Pragmata, another critical and financial hit, has grown its tally to 2.7m copies, more than double what it sold in its first two days of release. Resident Evil Requiem, meanwhile, has now surpassed 8.5m copies sold.

As part of the same report, Capcom also recorded its highest-ever number of unit sales for the first half of any fiscal year. This is attributed to Capcom's strong back-catalogue of titles, and regular sales and discounts.

But Capcom did not reference Monster Hunter Wilds sales at all in the report. The publisher did not share updated sales for the game, despite sharing a milestone for predecessor Monster Hunter: World, which is now well past 30m copies sold.

Although Wilds was incredibly successful at launch, the game's player base tapered off dramatically shortly afterwards. Capcom offered a sales update in last year's version of the same report, where it was revealed that MH Wilds had sold close to 11m copies overall, but the publisher hasn't offered an update since.

What does this mean - have sales slowed so significantly as to not be worth mentioning? Perhaps. But given that Wilds is coming to Switch 2 this December, and with the Ascendance expansion due for release next year, there's fuel in the tank yet.

It's impossible to overstate just how influential The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time has been since it launched on the Nintendo 64 back in 1998. It defined what 3D action-adventure games would look and play like for decades – not just in the Zelda series, but across all video games. As it turns out, this was part of the reason series producer Eiji Aonuma wanted to create the upcoming Ocarina of Time remake: he wanted to be sure the younger developers on the Zelda team understood just how important it was.

"Many of the team members who work alongside me on Legend of Zelda games today have only experienced developing the more recent titles," Aonuma explains in a new Ask the Developer interview from Nintendo. "That led me to wonder, 'Do they truly understand just how significant The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time was to the series as a whole?'"

Aonuma admits that, "of course, there are team members who vaguely know the game, and those who played it in their childhood days. But I started to wonder how they'd interpret The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time as they go about developing future Legend of Zelda games."

In part two of the interview, several of those younger developers explain their own history with Ocarina of Time. Some did have childhood memories of the game, while others had no experience with the original. "I played the Nintendo 64 version for the first time after joining this project," art director Aya Shida explains, "and I was amazed that a game this polished had been created 28 years ago."

"By learning the game structure and development style behind the original The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time," Aonuma explains, "and by actually rebuilding it as a full remake, it may trigger new insights that they can carry forward into future development. If we could achieve that, I thought it would be incredibly valuable. That's what led us to the conclusion that now is the right time to revisit The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time once again."

I'm excited by that rationale. The Zelda series hit severely diminishing returns by following closely the blueprint that Ocarina of Time laid out, and while Twilight Princess and Skyward Sword are both great games, there's no denying that they had less of an impact than the N64 classic. Zelda wouldn't feel truly fresh again until Breath of the Wild revamped the entire format of the series, but I fear that more open-world games are going to quickly get stale.

Maybe a synthesis of fresh and familiar ideas from a new generation of Zelda devs is just what the series needs. While Aonuma first joined the Zelda team by assisting on Ocarina of Time, it sounds like he wasn't too precious about these younger devs making changes to his baby. In fact, he wanted them to be even more bold – at least at first.

Sign up to our Switch 2 Spotlight newsletter to make sure you get the very latest news on Nintendo's new console and its games every week

"Looking at what they ultimately created," Aonuma explains, "I'm impressed by how rich an experience they were able to craft from a game that first came out 28 years ago. At the beginning of development, I remember thinking, 'They could be making more changes.' But as the project went on, it really came across just how deeply this development team cared about the original game, far more than we had imagined."

Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake had a Breath of the Wild quality-of-life feature until the series producer made devs take it out because it ruined "important" moments

He's been covering games (with occasional dalliances in the worlds of anime and pro wrestling) since 2015, first as a freelancer, then as a news writer at PCGamesN for nearly five years. His love for games was sparked somewhere between Metal Gear Solid 2 and Knights of the Old Republic, and these days you can usually find him splitting his entertainment time between retro gaming, the latest big action-adventure title, or a long haul in American Truck Simulator.

#3901. Don't worry, GTA 6's cars can drive for ages before their fuel tanks need refilling, leaving me wondering why this motor management's been added at all

Right, before you groan too hard, I promise that after I write this I'll take a break of indeterminate length from writing articles which amount to wondering aloud why a thing that's in GTA 6 is in GTA 6. Cars which need refuelling. It's not an addition there'd not been any hint was coming before today, as with the smell reaction system, leaks having hinted at fuel management all the way back in August.

Since that point, it's been confirmed as in the version of the game Rockstar will be shipping to consoles (boo) next month and PC at some point after that. Edge's GTA 6 long read notes the existence of fuel gauges and engine health readouts, but it also caveats them in what seems an insistence from Rockstar that the first of these features isn't designed to make filling up something the player necessarily has to do often or spend much time on when they do.

GTA 6's cars, according to Edge, can drive vast distances before they reach the point of running low on fuel, while refuelling is something you can do in quick and fuss-free fashion. On one hand, having cars that can barely drive three streets without sputtering to a halt and making the gas station experience a clunky chore that takes ages clearly would've both been terrible moves.

However, the fact the system's lenience is being emphasised has me wondering why it was worth adding at all. To be fair, Edge do outline that the variable amounts of gas in tanks does work with other new mechanics to add more unpredictability to crime sprees and rewards taking a bit more time to prepare a battle plan for robberies. If there's a chance that random ride you'd usually nick from an NPC on running out into the street with your loot might be running on fumes that won't get you through the ensuing police chase, that makes having proper getaway arrangements made prior to the stick-up more important. Then again, it seems any weapons your character's not got room to carry at any time are stored in their car's trunk in GTA 6 - rather than just shoved in pockets that can somehow fit an RPG - so always bringing your own wheels along on a job might be a no-brainer regardless.

All that in mind, this fuel management feels to me like it might suffer a fate similar to vampire RPG The Blood of Dawnwalker's time mechanics. If you've not played Dawnwalker - you should, here's my review - its devs Rebel Wolves based their story around giving the player 30 days and nights in which to find a way to save their family, lest mysterious consequences occur. Cue some folks feeling put off by the idea their adventuring would be restricted by any sort of time constraints, others concluding that the timer was too lenient to fulfil its role of focusing them on getting their task done in suitably rapid fashion, and people like me feeling like they had about the right amount of days left by the time they were in position to launch one of the game's final missions.

Managing fuel in games, especially ones in which people are used to being able to just get in a car and drive for as long as they fancy, tends to be similarly polarising. I can see some GTA 6 players raging against the idea that they've ever got to stop rampaging or partying to do something as mundane as fill up. I can see others being disappointed that, in trying to ensure that first group aren't put off, Rockstar have diluted the mechanic to the point it's not forcing players to fill up at a cadence that feels realistic in the way features like this are supposed to at their best. Many may end up thinking an ideal compromise has been reached. This can be the case with any feature in any game to a degree and all of us should at least try a game in the form its devs envisioned before resorting to moaning for more options or seeking out mods.

Though, as the driving games out there already prove, when it comes to fuel simulation it's usually best for studios to go all-in on committing to the mechanic if they're going to implement it, rather than trying to occupy a mushy middle ground. In full-blown sims like either of SCS's truck sims, SnowRunner, and iRacing, it's an obvious inclusion because the central appeal of those games lies in mirroring motoring in realistic detail. In open-world arcade racers like Forza Horizon, Need For Speed, and Burnout, it's usually cast aside as the sort of thing that'd be more of an annoying limitation than a welcome wrinkle, with filling stations that do appear often limited to dishing out nitrous or boost for extra speed instead.

Up until now, GTA's always fallen on the latter side of the fence and honestly seemed at home there. It's been an action-filled crime romp, not a life sim, and its cars have been designed to best suit that identity. With 6, though, Rockstar are skewing harder into the latter, as they did with Red Dead Redemption 2. RDR2's beloved, the majority of players could well end up adjusting to or appreciating this extra layer of thinking they'll have to do whenever they fire up their wheels. In my estimation, however, fuel management's the biggest risk Rockstar are taking with any of their new additions. The series is called Grand Theft Auto, after all. You're only messing with a wheeled aspect of it so central that they're right there in the name.

#3900. Tales of Tuscany launches February 22, 2027

Tales of Tuscany, a “WarioWare-soaked open-world RPG” follow-up to the 2024-released Athenian Rhapsody, will launch for PlayStation 5, Xbox Series, Switch, PC via Steam, iOS, and Android on February 22, 2027, publisher Top Hat Studios and developer Nico Papalia announced.

Here is an overview of the game, via Top Hat Studios:

Tuscany has been obliterated by the evil wizard Thunder Goober for his own personal entertainment! Play as Lambypoo and adventure through the broken land of Tuscany, either making friends and having them join your team or defeating enemies for their EXP in your efforts to save your cousins and reunite Tuscany…

Each journey through Tuscany is completely unique to the player at the wheel, and you’ll be awarded something called a Rhapsody each time you complete the game—a postcard which details your entire playthrough which you can trade cross-platform between friends! You’re tasked with reuniting Tuscany, but nobody is telling you how… do whatever you want!

Tales of Tuscany is a fast-paced, hilarious RPG where you control your own story. Build a team of misfits to take on bosses with and make choices that shape the world around you! Features include…

Bla Bla Bla I’m a Sheep. Alright I Get That Part. What is Like, the Actual Story?

#3899. Here are our PS Plus monthly games for November 2026

Dead Island 2! Tomb Raider! Monster Train 2!

Sony has announced the monthly games coming to PlayStation Plus Premium and Extra next month, bringing a mix of triple-A bangers and remastered classics to the service on the 3rd November. All are, of course, coming at the start of what is almost certainly going to be the biggest month of the year releases-wise.

Perhaps the biggest game on offer is Dead Island 2, Dambuster Studios and Deep Silver's first person zombie action game. There's plenty of grisly goodness here, and ample loot to snatch up and use against the undead hordes. It's a decent enough game, which should offer plenty of entertainment to those looking for something chunky to dig their teeth into while the Halloween spirit still lingers.

The remastered Tomb Raider Darkness Trilogy is not one to be skipped, especially if you're looking for a sizable time sink from your PlayStation Plus monthly games. While not known as being exactly the best Lara Croft games out there, Aspyr did some fine work polishing them up for modern platforms.

Finally we've got Monster Train 2. A deckbuilder roguelike that has you operating and managing trains where the forces of heaven and hell reside, all to defeat titans that threaten the orderly state of things. As the sole indie release on this monthly selection of PlayStation Plus games, it may be worth a try for those who can't get enough from the Roguelike genre even now. It even features a smug looking mushroom fella, how can you go wrong with that.

The reveal of these games coming to PlayStation Plus means the clock is ticking to grab October's offerings, many of which would fit well on the console of those getting into the spooky season.

Back in the '10s, Yacht Club cultivated a reputation as the studio that kept on giving—Shovel Knight Treasure Trove morphed into one of the best deals in the platformer genre, with one free update after another (including full story campaigns) for those who owned the original NES throwback.

But those awaiting the studio's follow-up, Mina the Hollower, spent a long time waiting, and delays left the company in dire need of a hit. "It’s make-or-break for sure," studio co-founder Cris Velasco told Bloomberg last year. "If we sold even 200,000, that would be really, really great. If we sold, like, 100,000, that’s not so good."

Well, we're a few months out from the game's release, when it sold over 500,000 copies in a few weeks, and Yacht Club is to remain afloat "...for now," co-founder Sean Velasco said in a Reddit AMA (via Eurogamer).

The future looks relatively bright for the developer, as other answers in the thread discuss that Mina the Hollower is due for some big updates soon, including randomizer and speedrunning options, and that most of the team is at work on a 3D game. Designer Alec Faulkner didn't provide any details on the unannounced game, other than to say "it’s gonna be soooooooo awesome."

It's good to hear the studio has the wind back in its sails, and it probably helped that Mina was such a hit. It seems set to hold its own the GOTY conversation later this year—and PC Gamer contributing writer Kerry Brunskill gave it a spiffy 90% in their review, calling it "a gloriously gothic combination of ferocious combat and beautiful scenery." If you've had your fill of the game itself, though, there's always Mina's fighting game debut to look forward to.

It seems rumors that Sam Houser is just a "taste director" are bunk

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Rockstar's notoriously private co-founder and president, Sam Houser, hasn't said a whole lot in public about his involvement in the studio's forthcoming behemoth, GTA 6, leading to a fair degree of rumor and speculation that he's taken a backseat in the actual day-to-day creative decision-making. That is not true in the slightest, according to Rockstar North co-studio head and head of development, Rob Nelson.

Talking to Edge for its big GTA 6 cover story, Nelson put the idea of Houser being little more than a "taste director" ala record producer Rick Rubin to bed. Nelson's exact words are paraphrased by Edge's editors, but Nelson insists that Houser was involved with the initial conception and general direction of GTA 6 and that he's integrally linked to every aspect of the game's creative direction, dispelling any suggestion that he's simply overseeing the company and general vibe of the project without as much direct creative input as earlier GTA games.

"Sam and I will identify problems or issues that we then solve with and across the teams," says Nelson of Houser's involvement. Nelson also says he spends a couple of weeks with Houser every time there's a new milestone in GTA 6's development, and together they come up with feedback addressing nitty gritty stuff like lighting and audio to more fundamental issues involving game mechanics, tone, and narrative. The feedback is then sent to the relevant teams, who work through Nelson and Houser's list of issues before the process picks back up again.

Of course, with a map size rivaling GTA 4, GTA 5, and Red Dead Redemption 2 combined, and a world where "you can go anywhere, any random location, and so many people have thought about that location," there's no way any one person can have eyes on every single tiny little detail in the game, but it's clear that Houser remains a foundational creative influence in the GTA canon even more than 30 years later.

GTA 6 lets you break up Jason and Lucia if you want, and we can thank Red Dead Redemption 2's Arthur Morgan for the choice

Exclusive: Nicholas Hoult teases his upcoming heist-comedy and Superman sequel

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Nicholas Hoult says his How to Rob a Bank vigilante character and DC villain Lex Luthor have a lot more in common than you'd think.

"For both of them, I think there's this element of, like, the end goal," Hoult tells GamesRadar+, when asked how Ryan and Lex Luthor compare. "They got so fixated on it. And that was what was really interesting about playing Luthor in Man of Tomorrow – I don't want to give too much away about the movie – but how James Gunn has written the character. There's a lot for Lex to try and understand about himself and the world. And so that was interesting to play."

In How to Rob a Bank, Hoult plays Ryan, the leader of a group of masked vigilantes (played by Pete Davidson, Anna Sawai, and Rhenzy Feliz) who are social media famous for their elaborate bank-robbing schemes. Ryan, either via YouTube video or livestream, gives pretty thorough instructions on how to rob a bank, evade police, and a plethora of other illegal activities. The key difference between Ryan and Lex Luthor, however, is that Ryan is doing it for the greater good. Lex, as we saw in James Gunn's Superman, is a bit more self-involved...

Continues Hoult: "But I think it's fun to play characters that have got, like, this set goal and obsession because then it gives you a very clear path through the story and the scenes."

Man of Tomorrow sees Superman and Lex Luthor come together in order to defeat Braniac, a supervillain that the Man of Steel can't take on alone. Star Nathan Fillion previously said we’ll "learn more about who Lex Luthor is" in the upcoming DC sequel.

How to Rob a Bank hits theaters on November 13. Man of Tomorrow is out July 9, 2027. For more, check out our breakdown of all the upcoming DC movies and shows on the way in 2026 and beyond.

#3895. "This company has been driven into a wall for years" - Life is Strange studio Don't Nod faces unrest while teetering on insolvency

"For two years, employees have been living on the edge."

There's deep unrest at French studio Don't Nod - creator of Life is Strange, Remember Me, Vampyr, Banishers: New Eden, and most recently Aphelion - as it scrambles to restructure itself and guard against insolvency.

Indeed, an impassioned account of proceedings on French union Le Syndicat des Travailleureuses du Jeu Vidéo's website (via Rock, Paper, Shotgun) reveals Don't Nod has entered safeguard proceedings - a kind of last-ditch restructuring effort to stave off insolvency. It also reports that even though redundancies are being made,Don't Nod intends to finish making the in-development game codenamed P14, albeit relying more on outsourced development rather than its cut-down in-house team.

The report, which claims knowledge of a memo sent by Don't Nod CEO Oskar Guilbert, and of the goings-on of the Don't Nod employee representatives - the CSE - doubts whether Don't Nod will be able to finish the game. Apparently all of the studio's character artists, concept artists, most of its environment artists, most of its sound designers, game designers, level designers, programmers, producers, testers, and dev-ops have been let go.

"To compensate for this massacre and keep on running with production on a game that, to this day, didn't cut down on its scope and is keeping around a hundred persons busy, management is betting it all on outsourcing," the report says.

"Managers, who are usually seen as more competent and experienced than non-managers, are kept within the organisation and studio management expects them to orchestrate the massive shift to outsourcing as well as take over the workload of the fired team members. Anyone with a little experience with video games production and sanity understands how out-of-touch such a plan is."

The report also claims Don't Nod management isn't able to offer affected staff severance packages or redundancy plans. "It'll be the strict legal minimum and you'll be glad for it," the report said. A voluntary redundancy scheme also isn't reportedly being offered.

"This company has been driven into a wall for years, against all outsider wisdom, against any sort of reality-based assessment," the report went on. "For two years, employees have been living on the edge, in uncertainty and anxiety, all of it reinforced by internal comms that alternated between inexistence and outright lies. This impacted their health, as evidenced by the CSE who documented six workplace accidents in 2026 and recently had to launch an inquiry into a serious and imminent danger.

"They do not care about the damage it deals to employees' health, they made no risk prevention plan. Employees feel like hostages to a radicalised management, who keep playing with the livelihood and the future of 140 people with no care for the consequences of their actions."

The CSE negotiations apparently end on 3rd November. We've asked Don't Nod for a comment.

News of Don't Nod's slide towards the brink of insolvency comes a month after the company's board voted to enter a period of restructuring - of transformation - that could lead to lay-offs for as many as 90 people. That in turn came only a few months after Don't Nod said it was close to running out of money.

The company's most recent game, Aphelion (released in April) - which charted a duo's escape across a sci-fi world - struggled to find an audience. We didn't review it on Eurogamer but a brief look around shows it only received middling scores. 2025's Life is Strange follow-up Lost Records fared better - we awarded it four out of five stars - but its success wasn't enough to properly propel the studio.

Top Hat Studios will publish Innombrable-developed 3D action adventure game Ryn: And the Thread of Life when it launches for PC via Steam, the companies announced. A release date was not announced.

Here is an overview of the game, via its Steam page:

The world is unraveling: The dark witch Stella has torn the sacred Thread of Life, and now magic bleeds in corrupt shreds.

As Ryn, a rag doll born from the last fragment of light, journey through the dying heart of a withering realm. Each step reveals new challenges, horrors… and new powers.

The five wicked dolls guard the stolen fragments. Defeat their nightmares, master their abilities, and reweave fate with the edge of your magical scissors!

Fast, fluid, and visceral hack-and-slash combat keeps the action moving in constant motion. Chain light and heavy attacks, dodge with precision, and unleash powerful abilities stolen from fallen enemies.

Quick Time Events turn battles into cinematic showdowns that demand reflexes, and reward skill. Every strike with Ryn’s enchanted scissors doesn’t just wound… it cuts through destiny itself!

Dive into a retro-inspired interconnected platforming world, where every area is filled with secrets, shortcuts, and hidden paths.

Discover the stories and tribulations that tore this realm apart. Scour over every nook and cranny for unlockables, diaries, and experience rich environmental storytelling.

To confront the evil Witch Stella, you must first vanquish the five corrupted dolls that guard her domain. Each hard-fought victory strips away her influence, and provides powerful new abilities to claim as your own.

These gifts grant not only the strength to crush Stella’s minions, but also the tools to uncover what was once unreachable – opening new areas, hidden paths, and the methods to reveal new secrets within familiar territory.

#3893. Queen's Domain is a brilliant King's Field-alike RPG that forces you to walk so you can learn to fly

I would also have accepted "Prince's Place" or "Baron's Turf"

FromSoftware's elderly King's Field games aren't really celebrated for their feeling of agility. They are glorious first-person trudgefests, a treacle-thick waltz of swinging and spellcraft, with players wobbling in and out of attack range like British men who aren't sure whether the other man wants a hug. Unlike in the later Dark Souls action-RPGs, to which King's Field owes some of its retrospective popularity, there's no dodge-roll to grease the wheels.

Out this week on Steam, Queen's Domain is often as ponderous as King's Field, but it's also an exercise in steady, triumphant acceleration. Ultimately, it wants you to fly. To this end, it equips you - well, once you've boshed a huge skeleton sentinel - with a fancy windblade that lets you perform an aerial dash, speeding your manouevres while allowing you to reach new areas.

You'll find socketable gems that extend the dash, gradually bringing offshore islands and collapsed castle parapets within reach. I'm around four hours into Queen's Domain, and right now, the overall objective is tricking out that enchanted blade: heading down one leg of a marvellous, knotty world, retrieving a gem, and returning along another path, while keeping an eye out for nooks and platforms that once seemed like cordoned-off backdrop.

While an obvious quick-select default, the windblade doesn't make the 50 or so other weapons in the game obsolete, partly because enemies are distinguished by damage type: skellingtons are tougher against swords, while spears tend to bounce off malformed rodent ladybugs. All the weapons level up with use, and all of them have special abilities: the first spear you acquire has a retreating stab, useful against grasshopper chickens with lunging kicks, while the basic wooden club has a pounce move, skipping the lengthy swinging animation that is the weapon's major disadvantage.

For all these flourishes, combat is often as reassuringly stodgy as I remember King's Field being on the early PlayStation consoles. The pace is set by the need to charge your attacks, holding the button till the wind-up consumes your whole stamina bar; spamming blows is much less efficient.

350 words in, and I haven't mentioned the standout attraction in Queen's Domain – the landscape itself, an absurdly lovely expanse of mossy arches, chopped pillars and racked tombs that evokes Shadow of the Colossus and Vagrant Story as much as it does FromSoftware. It's a beautiful place, a haunting recovery of PS2 aesthetics that runs comfortably on integrated graphics. Or at least, it's beautiful until you start screwing around with focal length and lurid filters in the Photo Mode (see below).

The archipelago's interwoven paths are structured around save crystals where you can rest at the price of respawning enemies, but unlike in Souls, enemies eventually respawn of their own accord, appearing in different combinations as you pass certain milestones.

If this last wrinkle creates more potential for ambush, you can shape encounters using your secondary weapons, beginning with a belt of throwing daggers hanging from a shipwreck. I specify the location because embarrassingly, I managed to overlook them for the first hour – in general, Queen's Domain doesn't highlight collectible objects as flagrantly as certain recent blockbusters.

You get an endless supply of daggers, governed by a cooldown. The best thing about them initially is that you can use them to murder the highly annoying laser eyeballs that deck the tree trunks, often zapping you in the back while you're battling something else. Beyond that, you'll use them to bait individuals away from mobs, luring them towards killzones with plenty of strafing room, or getting them jammed behind monoliths so that you can bop their noggins at leisure.

I've got over 30 hours of Queen's Domain left to burn, according to devs Freshly Baked. Unlike with a lot of the non-review games I've dipped into this year, I feel like I might actually go the distance. More thoughts to follow, possibly! If you're new to King's Fieldalikes, you may find this stifling and frustrating at first. Even if you do know your King's Fields, you'll likely perish a lot. But hopefully, the landscape's magnificence and the increasing swagger of the combat system will get you over the hump. The game launches tomorrow, and there's still a demo on Steam as of writing.

As reported by MMORPG.com, Square Enix has delayed Final Fantasy 14's Evercold expansion to February 2 from its initial January launch window. Preorders for the add-on will open up on Wednesday, November 4⁠—those preorders also come with early access to the expansion on February 19.

The news was delivered by FF14 honcho Naoki "Yoshi-P" Yoshida at the opening day of Final Fantasy 14's 2026 Fan Festival in Tokyo. Yoshi-P explained that the team was committed to its January window, and were even "just barely" on track to meet that schedule. Quality concerns led Yoshi-P to make the call on three extra weeks of development time.

One month isn't enormous in the context of most game development these days, but it is fairly impactful for the audience and overall pace of updates in a live service concern like Final Fantasy 14. Evercold will be the first new expansion for Final Fantasy 14 since the release of Dawntrail in July, 2024.

From the outside, Final Fantasy 14 has struck me as one of the more high-morale MMO communities out there, but I was permanently scarred by peak pandemic, Season of the Worthy Destiny, so my standards might be pretty low. In her 2025 state of the game writeup at the beginning of the Dawntrail era, PCG features producer Mollie Taylor observed that FF14 was in "a pretty weird spot."

But Mollie seems cautiously optimistic for Evercold's promised changes, while a recent roguelike mode added to FF14 has news writer Harvey Randall excited for the upcoming expansion's combat overhaul. Its new class looks pretty dope as well: A viking with two shields, laser cannons, and Wolverine claws.

Super Mario Bros. players have spent years trying to build the perfect speedrun. The race to be the first to achieve the perfect run has escalated dramatically over the past year, and the now-legendary Niftski has just set a new record that's just two frames away from the entire community's ultimate goal. The catch? He didn't actually want to do it – at least not when he did.

"My supporters donated $1,000 for me to do a Mario impression" for an entire Halloween stream, as Niftski explains in the description of his record run on YouTube. He dutifully completed the stream dressed in a Mario hat and fake mustache while doing what he recognizes as "the worst Mario impression of all time."

The entire video is an absolute delight as Niftski slowly recognizes that he's on world record pace while wearing a silly costume and doing a silly voice. "Finally, I just-a had to-a lock in," he says as he warps into level 4-1. The faux facial hair starts to bother him in 4-2, as he complains that "I want to shave-a this thing off because it's-a literally freaking uncomfortable as hell-a."

"I really hope this run dies, by the way," he says as he enters the game's final stages, still on pace for that record. By level 8-3, the penultimate stage, he's getting desperate. "Please have this-a run die," he begs, "I don't-a like it, I don't-a want to get this larping as Mario."

Yet he does indeed secure the world record while-a doing a Mario voice. "It made me not nervous at all," he recognizes, and that might've been the push he needed to set the new record. Still, there are two more frames to shave away before the perfect speedrun finally arrives, and I can only imagine what lengths Niftski might have to go to in order to calm his nerves again.

#3890. Celeste and TowerFall have been removed from the Xbox store in a move to "support the BDS boycott" against Microsoft

This follows fellow indie dev House House announcing Big Walk will not be coming to Xbox

It's a good day to love Celeste! Earlier today it was discovered that Celeste had been removed from the Xbox Store while it remained on the PlayStation and Nintendo digital storefronts. Now, as shared by the game's co-creator Maddy Thorson, it's been confirmed that both Celeste and TowerFall were removed from store expressly in support of the BDS called boycott against Xbox over Microsoft providing support to the Israeli military as it enacts its genocide of the Palestinian people.

A larger statement hasn't been made by other Celeste developers or Thorson's current studio EXOK Games, but the larger more important point is that the games are no longer available for purchase on the Xbox Store. Earlier this month, House House, developer of one of the biggest indies of the year Big Walk, also shared their own support for the BDS movement and Microsoft boycott announcement by announcing their (quite excellent) social puzzle game will not be launching on Xbox for the foreseeable future. Developer Origame Digital also made an incredibly potent statement denouncing the genocide in their latest game, Penguin's Colony.

For those who’re asking, yes we delisted Celeste and TowerFall on XBox. We did this to support the BDS boycott

For those not in the know, BDS called for the boycott of Microsoft and Xbox games and hardware last year over the tech company providing AI software to the Israeli military which was used specifically to target Palestinian civilians; Microsoft have even confirmed that they were providing this software. They remain on the BDS boycott list due to the fact they continue to provide the Israeli military with other services such as email and file management systems, as well as for "combat and intelligence activities."

The actions of EXOK Games, House House and Origame Digital come at a time of a growing pushback against Xbox over Microsoft's support of the military movement, in part from No Games for Genocide, an organisation made up of developers and industry practitioners (disclaimer: I myself am an organiser at NGFG). These actions show how possible it is to express solidarity with the Palestinian people, and are a good example to follow.

#3889. Cyberpunk 2 might include multiplayer after CD Projekt Red scrapped the feature in Cyberpunk 2077

Cyberpunk 2 might try to revive Cyberpunk 2077's online ambitions, as a new CD Projekt Red job listing is looking for someone familiar with "multiplayer network architecture."

As spotted by Cheap Happens, the role-playing powerhouse is currently looking to hire a lead quest programmer for its upcoming open-world sequel. Buried away at the bottom of the job listing, under the "Nice To Haves" section, the studio asks for an "understanding of multiplayer network architecture and client-server synchronization for game state/ quests."

The multiplayer mention is by no means confirmation that Cyberpunk 2 - or whatever it ends up being called - will have co-op and other online modes, but it's definitely something CD Projekt Red is looking into. And it certainly makes sense, too.

Once upon a time, Cyberpunk 2077 was intended to receive a multiplayer portion sometime after its initial launch. Of course, at the time, the shaky state of the game's development meant that was no longer feasible and CD Projekt Red instead said multiplayer would come as its own "triple-A release." Eventually, the famed studio realised it simply had to focus on ensuring the base game was stable enough on its own, and shelved those online ambitions.

A few years back, Cyberpunk 2077's senior quest designer, Philipp Weber, told Eurogamer the company was "focusing on bringing online into all of our franchises one day" by "building an online technology that can be seamlessly integrated into development of our future games."

More recently, in 2024, CD Projekt CEO Adam Badowski said the team were "considering" multiplayer elements for the Cyberpunk sequel back when the game was still in its early concept phases.

We don't know much else about the neon-drenched follow-up, but CDPR has been keeping series fans full and fed with continual updates to Cyberpunk 2077. Earlier this week, the game got an update celebrating the debut of Cyberpunk Edgerunners Season 2 on Netflix - everything from dual-wielding to cross-platform mods were added to the six-year-old game.

Earlier this month, Big Walk developer House House explained why their co-op puzzle adventure wouldn't be available for sale on Xbox: Microsoft's gaming division is a priority target of the the Palestinian-led BDS (Boycott, Divestment, Sanctions) movement, which names the tech giant in general as a pressure target alongside Google, Amazon, and a host of other companies. House House isn't alone in taking this action.

Narrative platformer Celeste and party fighter TowerFall have delisted from Xbox recently, and Maddy Thorson of Maddy Makes Games fame took to BlueSky to explain why: "For those who’re asking, yes, we delisted Celeste and TowerFall on Xbox. We did this to support the BDS boycott."

For reference, Microsoft gets a cut whenever it makes a sale through its proprietary digital distribution storefront, similar to Steam. Console producers tend to take a loss on hardware, subsidizing it for accessibility to more consumers, so they can make up the difference by selling other stuff, a crucial slice of that other stuff being games.

So as long as sales trickle in for critically acclaimed games like Celeste and TowerFall, that's a bit of easy money for Microsoft—the choice to delist the game stops that. If you're an Xbox owner who wants to observe the boycott, you can always buy used physical versions of games where that's an option or switch to another platform for the time being.

But this is PC Gamer dot com, so you probably haven't even heard of the Xbox. You've certainly never seen one up close. You're probably playing Chessmaster 9000 on your second monitor as you read this, you beautiful freak. In any case, you can always buy TowerFall on Steam. Same goes for Celeste.

Helen Chiang has "serious concerns" about Microsoft's handling of her departure

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Helen Chiang, the Microsoft veteran and former Xbox COO who left the company in October, is pushing back on reports claiming she was fired for violating company policy.

In an impassioned rebuttal posted on LinkedIn, Chiang directly refutes a recent report from Eurogamer that claimed she had been fired from Microsoft for policy violations. "That’s not accurate and while I won’t turn this into a play-by-play, silence should not be mistaken for agreement," says Chiang.

"What has been said about my departure, and what has been left unsaid, has created a picture of me that I hardly recognize. It’s important to me to set the record straight."

Refuting claims point by point, Chiang says she didn't leak confidential information to the press, she didn't leave Xbox to join a competitor, "did not engage in discrimination, bullying, harassment, insider trading, embezzlement, or other fraudulent activity," and didn't leave because she was passed up for a bigger role. The reason for Chiang's departure hasn't been made clear, neither by Chiang nor Microsoft. At the time of the departure, Xbox CEO Asha Sharma said she was "grateful for her years of service" and wished Chiang well in a surprisingly brief message to employees.

"I believe in fairness, accountability, and holding ourselves to the standards we expect of others," she says. "Those standards only mean something when they’re applied consistently. I have serious concerns about how they were applied in my case, and I believe those concerns deserve to be taken seriously.

"I share this because I don’t want my departure reduced to an inaccurate story about incompetence, ambition for the next big job, or a Nelson-level scandal. My story is about staying true to your core values, especially when it is hard. That’s the legacy I hope to leave behind."

The full details of Chiang's departure might never come into view, but the abrupt removal of a 21-year veteran is noteworthy. Chiang joined Microsoft in 2005 as product manager and worked her way up to studio head and then corporate vice president of the Minecraft franchise in 2020. Sharma was appointed as Xbox's first COO by Sharma in July as part of the company's big "reset".

#3885. The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel will be an Elder Scrolls game about the infinite mysteries of the Elder Scrolls, report with some plot hintage claims

Also, it's claimed to be set in the place most heavily rumoured since that 2018 teaser

As Xbox's execs continue to pine for game-related announcements to fill in the gaps between their rounds of mass layoffs, The Elder Scrolls 6 is reportedly set to gain the subtitle Sentinel soon. That's according to a report which also includes some details of where the game that's long been a twinkle in the eye of Skyrim's dad will be set and what its plot will involve.

According to The Verge, The Elder Scrolls VI: Sentinel could be getting some sort of re-reveal in November that'll lock that in as its full title. Skyrim turns 15 on November 11th, so if Bethesda are looking for a date with some TES significance to it, that one would fit the bill.

Beyond the name, the report points to Hammerfell as the game's setting, something the aforementioned name being confirmed would make obvious if you're an Elder Scrolls nerd like me and know that Sentinel is the name of both a kingdom and city in the Redguards' province. As far as I recall, Hammerfell's also been the setting a majority of fans have believed most likely since that infamous TES 6 teaser in 2018, with some thinking a bit of nearby province and Daggerfall setting High Rock might also be included if the game's map spans the Iliac Bay region.

For now, it's deserty Hammerfell, baby. As for what you'll reportedly be up to there, the report points to The Emma Stones 6 having some secrets to explore linked to the mysterious provenance of the Elder Scrolls themselves. Yep, that's the magic bits of paper which blind people by slamming dangerous and unknowable knowledge into their brains, and can also be used for handy tasks like learning the shout needed to defeat Alduin. You're usually lugging a couple around by the time you've finished TES V, no doubt stuffed between cheese wheels in your massive backpack.

All in all, nothing I can see seems to suggest The Elder Scrolls 6 will deviate much from the sort of adventure Skyrim seemed to be teeing up, with the Thalmor-led Aldmeri Dominion on the march to conquer Tamriel and possibly get up to some metaphysical bollocks to return the land to a state resembling a previous era when elves were on top, if theories long-discussed among fans turn out not to be bunkum.

Such a setup would mirror what Skyrim co-lead designer Kurt Kuhlmann outlined earlier this year as the starting point for the direction he might've taken the game, if he'd helmed it rather than departing Bethesda in 2023.

To be honest, the only thing - aside from the Microsoft stink the game can't escape - that's giving me pause in getting too excited about the direction TES 6 seems to be headed in is that fact that the series' world has been left standing still for so long following Skyrim. I'm not saying it needs a reboot, but I am concerned that - ironically given the Elder Scrolls themselves are time-centric artifacts - this might feel like a game a bit out of time unless it can take a big step mechanically.

#3884. Alien: Isolation 2 devs commit to a physical edition: "Staying true to the analogue nature of Alien is one of our pillars"

And the Xenomorph's "even more intelligent" this time.

The developers behind Alien: Isolation 2 are committing to a full physical edition, and have shared even more details about the highly-anticipated survival horror sequel.

In a recent developer Q&A posted today (below), developers from Creative Assembly shed even more light on their shadowy follow-up to 2014's fan-favorite horror game. When asked if the sequel would get a physical edition, the devs simply said "yes" and explained that "staying true to the analogue nature of Alien is one of our pillars."

Throughout the video, the Creative Assembly team reiterated that so much of their inspiration comes from Ridley Scott's seminal sci-fi classic from 1979, naturally, which influenced their decision to release a physical boxed version of the game and to keep the focus on one ever present, highly intelligent and always frightening Xenomorph.

Confirmation of a physical release comes months after Sony announced plans to end production of new PlayStation discs in 2028 - a decision that led to heated backlash from players, physical distributors and consumer rights groups.

The only wrinkle is that Alien: Isolation 2 doesn't have a release date at the moment. Should it release any later than February, 2028, PlayStation players probably won't be able to get their hands on a proper disc - though the game is also launching across PC, Nintendo Switch 2 and Xbox Series X/S.

Elsewhere in the dev vlog, creative director Al Hope explained how the team is expanding on the original game's famously tight level design. "You have the interior spaces which feel claustrophobic and the player feels trapped, which is super familiar to Isolation fans. But we also have exteriors as well where the creature is now learning to adapt and hunt in these open spaces," Hope said.

"I really love the idea that the player will feel trapped and claustrophobic in the interiors and actually really want to get outside. Once they manage to do that, after that initial relief and sense of a small victory, they will start very slowly to feel really exposed and vulnerable and actually quite like to go back inside again. And really, playing on that roller coaster and see-saw of emotion and motivation - that's a big part of what Alien: Isolation 2 is."

James Green, lead game designer, also said roughly "a quarter to a third of the team worked on the original," while all new developers helped to bring a fresh perspective onboard. And, somehow, the Xenomorph is "even more intelligent" this time; scarily capable of using the extreme climate to hide and hunt you.

#3882. Dark visual novel PRIMA MATERIA announced for PC

Publisher Top Hat Studios and Synergia developer Radi Art have announced PRIMA MATERIA, a dark visual novel coming to PC via Steam in 2027.

Here is an overview of the game, via Top Hat Studios:

PRIMA MATERIA is a dark surreal visual novel set in a sterilized wasteland ruled by Angels, where consciousness is harvested, brewed, and sold. Mana, a Mind Digger who survives by eating minds, takes one last job: fixing a demi-angel worth keeping whole.

“I must reject morality because it serves those in power; this is a mechanical world where I am nothing but a mechanical device and so is everyone else. Everything’s real, nothing’s in your head.”

In the Concrete Sea, an endless grey wasteland beneath a sun that never sets, consciousness is a resource. Angels farm humans for it, brewing it over centuries into Prima Materia, a luminous orange liquid that can be distilled and most importantly, consumed. Mana is a Mind Digger, someone who carves psyches for a living, extracting and eating what others don’t want to carry anymore: guilt, fear, memories.

Her self-contained existence collapses with the arrival of Girin: the rebellious daughter of an ancient Angel, dropped at Mana’s door with a simple request to “fix” her, in exchange for an infinite supply of Prima Materia. Girin’s untamable nature doesn’t make things easy, but it’s what lies deep inside her mind that scares Mana. Something old and protective is waiting, something that recognizes Mana for what she is and that has no interest in letting her anywhere near Girin’s core.

What begins as a transaction quickly becomes something stranger, more intimate, and far more dangerous. Because the deeper Mana digs, the more she finds the memory of the person she was before she carved herself down to appetite and survival.

#3881. It sounds like you shouldn't expect Destiny 2's campaign unvaulting to be ready until 2028, as Bungie tease their plans for the future of the series

When Bungie announced that they would be ceasing to work on major updates for Destiny 2 earlier this year, it obviously felt like that was the end of that, and any future games were not guaranteed whatsoever. Then last month, they announced that they'll be bringing back all of the shooter's vaulted campaigns, which is obviously a lot of work! Now, in a blog post, the developer has outlined where they're at with this process, offering up a timeline of when to expect the unvaulted campaigns, what will be included with them, and light teases for whatever comes after that.

"Our first pass for unvaulting, available to all players, focuses on getting our campaign slate whole again," head of product Josh Deane explains in the blog post. "We're specifically targeting the activity content of Campaigns, Strikes, and Raids from vaulted expansions. Menagerie holds a special place in our hearts (and we've seen years of community requests for a return), so it will be a part of this pass as well." In practical terms, that means the return of the Red War, Forsaken, Curse of Osiris and Warmind campaigns, strikes, raids and raid lairs from said campaigns, and Menagerie Activity with reprised rewards.

The process for this unvaulting apparently began in June as the team scoped the feasibility of it all, and as of now it's pre-production. Full-on production is expected to start in February 2027 at the latest, but it's worth noting that this is expected to take about 12 months to wrap up. That means you won't be jumping back into any of these beloved expansions until 2028 at least, by the sounds of things.

The team also has "stretch goals" that they're investigating for either the unvaulting launch or sometime after, specifically for things like free roam destinations, seasonal activities from Sundial (season 9) to The Coil (season 32), raid and raid lair weapon updates, and PvP maps.

There are seemingly bigger plans for the game too, with some kind of "celebration" to come beyond Moment of Triumph with "new updates", and something referred to as Destiny 'Legacy'; "Our epic journey started over a decade ago, and the whole experience needs to be served to you all where you play today. Expect more information when we come back to you all early next year." Certainly sounds like they're talking about the original Destiny here, but I suppose we should take that with a pinch of salt. Lastly, they mention "Redacted," which is accompanied by this line, "Launch Ventrilo Message: 'We’re back'". No idea what that means, I'll leave that to you Destiny-heads.

Essentially, the core message seems to be that Bungie are "building a new future for Destiny," so, it's not totally dead in the water. You can expect the next major comms update from Bungie in February, too.

The case as presented by Rebelzize seems fairly open and shut: A volunteer team being sued by a former volunteer over contributions excised from the project? I have questions, but ideally this whole situation will resolve cleanly enough that we never know exactly what happened:

At last call, Skyblivion was still scheduled to release this year, but time is running short for that goal. We Elder Scrolls-likers at PC Gamer have been excited about it for years. Skyblivion promises a more ground-up remake of TES 4: Oblivion⁠—complete with radically redesigned dungeons and biomes⁠—in Skyrim's engine. #3879. Epic Games further doubles down on gen-AI tools for Fortnite, Unreal Engine 6 and more: "Our engineers are no longer writing the bulk of the code"

"We are more concerned about the risks of moving too slowly than we are about AI skepticism."

To no one's surprise, Epic Games has now confirmed that it's tripling down on its gen-AI push and will use the controversial tech on everything from Fortnite to the next iteration of its widely-used game development engine, Unreal Engine 6.

Speaking to This Week In Video Games, executive vice president of development Marcus Wassmer confirmed that "we are definitely using AI to develop code and features for Unreal Engine," but that work will also be extended to the engine's next big numbered version. "Almost all development happening right now is being done in the dev streams attached to Fortnite, UEFN [Unreal Editor for Fortnite], and UE6."

When asked specifically if Epic is vibe-coding anything related to Unreal Engine, Wassmer put it plainly: "Yes, we are vibe-coding things. That means our engineers are no longer writing the bulk of the code, but they are still guiding the tools to get the architectural result we want. We're not 'one-shotting' the engine; we're iterating with AI to ship features developers want and keep the engine within the memory, performance, and scalability envelopes." Wassmer claimed the AI tools would help the company push out updates faster and with fewer bugs.

Epic seemingly isn't sweating over the divisive reaction to its gen-AI push, either - even as workers worry about job security, developers worry about plagiarism, and communities across the world worry about its environmental impact. Wassmer explained the company is "more concerned about the risks of moving too slowly than we are about AI skepticism."

"We don't think it's viable to take a halfway approach to AI in development," he added. "We think it's best to just be up front with what we're doing, share best practices with other developers, and make the best UE6 we can with the best tools available at any given time."

Earlier this month, Epic proudly admitted to vibe-coding the latest iteration of the Epic Games Launcher in an attempt to run slightly faster than Steam. "Prograaming is hard," the multi-billion dollar company explained at the time. "So, instead of doing that, we vibe coded the new Epic Games Launcher." Developers working on a troubled Disney and Marvel shooter were reportedly told to let gen-AI handle code and art production, too.

Epic CEO Tim Sweeney then started an online debate over Valve's AI policy that asks developers to disclose gen-AI use on their Steam pages. Sweeney argued that "forcing developers to write a political statement to be used against them by the hate mod they're helping organize is abhorrent." It's not surprising to see Epic dig its heels in further, then.

The secret had "remained undiscovered for over 29 years"

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Elder Scrolls only started to find mainstream success between the releases of Morrowind and Oblivion, but Bethesda was keen on expanding the series into a franchise well before that point. The 1997 release of An Elder Scrolls Legend: Battlespire is rarely discussed these days, but it's been hiding a secret for over 29 years. Today, The Strong National Museum of Play has lifted the veil on a mysterious Easter egg that's been lost for decades.

If you're not familiar with Battlespire, it's essentially a linear dungeon crawler set in the world of the Elder Scrolls. It's still a first-person game that retains much of the crunchy RPG combat that defined Arena and Daggerfall, just within a much more constrained location. Battlespire's development was led by the "father of The Elder Scrolls," Julian LeFay, who died in 2025.

As documented on the Unofficial Elder Scrolls Pages wiki, players have known for some time that there's an Easter egg in Battlespire involving a photo featuring a photo of some members of the development team. "It is not currently known how to get this Easter egg to display or if it actually functions in the final game," the UESP wiki laments. However, the mystery has finally been solved thanks to The Strong Museum, which has recently received a set of documents that belonged to LeFay.

On the eve of Bethesda's 40th Anniversary, a sneak peek at The Strong Museum's Julian LeFay papers looks at an Easter egg from An Elder Scrolls Legend: Battlespire that has remained undiscovered for over 29 years.

As explained in a Bluesky video from Strong director Andrew Borman, if you load into the game and hold down the number 1 on your keyboard as you type the word "spire," the dev photo will pop up on screen along with the caption "Battlespire rules!"

The degree to which Battlespire rules is somewhat questionable, since it received mediocre reviews upon release and was jointly credited – alongside Redguard – as the start of a down period for Bethesda that the studio only recovered from with the success of Morrowind. But Battlespire was the final Elder Scrolls game LeFay worked on as a Bethesda employee (though he briefly did contract work on Morrowind) and in many ways marks the final chapter of the series' early format.

The fact that Battlespire still had secrets to reveal after all these years is remarkable, and it's a testament to the lasting impact of the world LeFay ushered into existence that people still care to uncover them.

Todd Howard joins fans mourning "the driving force in the creation of The Elder Scrolls and the foundations of Bethesda as a game studio," Julian LeFay: "Without Julian, we would not be here today"

#3876. After the rough start that was last year's entry, Football Manager 27 is looking to bring you in with a few free days of play before the game's even out

Football Manager 27 is still a good week and ahead out from launch, but if you're quick you can already get to playing it. That's because developer Sports Interactive have released a Launch Preview version of the game that lets you take it for a kickabout before it comes out in earnest.

As the devs explain in a Steam blog post, "running for the next five days, the FM27 Launch Preview will be freely playable," across all of its release platforms. "There’s no additional sign-up required, simply download from your preferred platform and begin turning your football vision into dugout decisions. This is your chance to get hands-on with the complete FM27 experience across all game modes, including Shuffle Draft, the fast-paced new multiplayer addition."

One caveat worth noting is that there may be some bugs or glitches in the game that the devs "will work to address in future updates." This, understandably, may be a touchy subject for some. It didn't exactly have a stellar launch, with early patches having to fix hundreds of bugs and other issues. Not that Steam reviews are the be all, end all, but the game is still sitting at a mostly negative a year on. It's very well possible that getting the new one in folks' hands early is a way to bring back some of the audience they may have lost last year.

Still, it doesn't sound like Football Manager 26 was all bad. Phil spent a lofty 227 hours on the game around when it launched, writing for RPS at the time, "That massive database of players, staff and clubs, layered so expertly over time with systems that make them all feel alive and dynamic, is still thrilling. It’s not a new feature by any stretch, but it feels overly punitive to discount it because the menus are bad and it chugs along whenever you press continue. It’s a bad version of a fundamentally great experience, and that means my brain’s going to be full of AS Roma matters for the foreseeable, no matter how many AI gravestones I see in my feed decrying the death of the series."

Dragon Age: The Veilguard is one of the more polarizing releases in the beloved RPG series' history despite largely positive reviews, with the writing and story in particular being the most contentious talking point among fans. If former series boss Mark Darrah could point to a reason, and if he carried himself with literally zero humility, he'd probably say it's because he left developer BioWare in 2021 and only served as a freelance consultant on Dragon Age: The Veilguard in the final stretch of development. The fact that he wasn't one of the project leads meant the developers were within their rights to simply ignore his suggestions, and according to Darrah, they frequently did do that.

"There were lots of things that I made recommendations on that were not listened to," Darrah tells Eldorado.gg. "And in fact, in some cases, I would make a recommendation, it was ignored, and then a different group that was also helping would make the same recommendation, and then it was listened to. So it was definitely a frustrating experience for me."

Darrah previously attributed the downfall of Dragon Age to BioWare's preference for "simpler" and "more accessible" RPGs, which he said prevented it from having a major hit like Baldur's Gate 3.

Dragon Age, not to mention Mass Effect and other BioWare franchises, are back in the news following EA's abrupt closure of the studio and cancelation of Mass Effect 5. And before you put the blame on any one game, developer, or team within BioWare, it's worth noting the recently completed $55 billion leveraged buyout of EA by Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund (PIF), private equity firm Silver Lake, and Jared Kushner's Affinity Partner.

#3874. More Chinese success as Phantom Blade Zero enjoys a big launch and becomes one of Steam's most played games

Phantom Blade Zero has been officially released, and just as everyone expected, it's popular. The wuxia action game from S-Game debuted to a massive 431,541 concurrent players on Steam (via SteamDB) at its peak just hours ago.

At the time of writing, Phantom Blade Zero is Steam's second most-played game, landing just below Counter-Strike 2, and it's currently leading Steam's global top sellers chart, having jumped 16 places this week. Players appear to be happy with the final game, too, judging by early user reviews on Steam, which currently have it sitting at a Mostly Positive average.

S-Game has yet to announce any sales figures, but the game was estimated to have sold more than 1m copies just before launch. According to Alinea Analytics analyst Rhys Elliott, Phantom Blade Zero sold 850,000 copies across PC and PlayStation 5. It is also available on Tencent WeGame in China, where Elliott estimates it sold enough to bring the total to well above 1m copies.

A few days earlier, Elliott estimated Phantom Blade Zero to have sold 500,000 on Steam. The analyst indicated that 80,000 copies were sold after reviews were published two days before the game's 28th October release. As impressive as all of that is, it pales in comparison to Black Myth: Wukong's sales performance - another Chinese-developed action title. When Wukong released in 2024, the game peaked at 2,415,714 concurrent players on Steam, and is estimated to have sold over 30m copies lifetime.

Elliott said on X he doesn't believe Phantom Blade Zero will be able to achieve that level of success, but he predicts strong sales this year regardless - which is already borne out by the available data.

Seeing as the game has benefited from the pre-launch hype, word of mouth may help boost these numbers further. By the weekend, we could be looking at well above 500,000 peak concurrents on Steam.

In Eurogamer's review of Phantom Blade Zero, Emma Kent lamented a general lack of polish and pace-breaking boss fights, which put a dampener on her enjoyment of the best parts of the game: swordplay and combat.
