#3722. Gay People (Mostly) Explain Gay Halloween

When you see a post that begins with “I hate gay Halloween, what do you mean you’re dressed as…” you know you’re in for a good laugh, or perhaps the feeling that you’re completely out of the loop. Trick-or-treating isn’t until this weekend, but in the age of social media the day itself has taken the back seat—it’s online where the battle for the best costumes takes place, and it’s happening earlier every year.

The trend began taking shape in the late 2010s and gained strength during the pandemic: celebrities—most notably the Kardashian-Jenner clan—began re-creating memorable moments from pop culture, mostly old film posters or iconic music album covers, and staging elaborate costume shoots for their Instagrams. The closer the re-creation would get to the original the better—and worthier of likes.

The idea of gay Halloween exists somewhere in this realm, though it’s inevitably more lo-fi, and the most successful looks aim for laughs rather than mere online clout. Plainly, it’s when people—mostly gay men—pick a niche pop culture moment or meme and re-create it in a costume. Forget witches and Scream masks. In 2004, Mean Girls declared, “In girl world, Halloween is the one night of the year when a girl can dress like a total slut and no other girls can say anything about it.” The 2026 equivalent is less about horny devils. Halloween is now the one night of the year when you can let out your inner freak or geek: Now you can be the breakup Post-it from a 2003 episode of Sex and the City, or Marc Jacobs when he wore a neck brace. Two years ago, a friend dressed as Antonio, a character played by Ariana Grande on Saturday Night Live. Another at the same party went as Rihanna as a nun for an Interview magazine cover.

Owen Thiele and Benito Skinner dressed as PinkPantheress and Zara Larsson for Halloween.

Once upon a time, Halloween was about being as frightening as possible. Sure, there is something indeed terrifying about being broken up with via Post-it, and some less-online people are still attached to the classics—a zombie, a devil, et cetera—but Halloween has been co-opted by the internet, and by celebrity culture, in a way that has made it entirely self-indulgent.

Consider Heidi Klum’s famous annual Halloween bash, which she started in 2000. Early on, her costumes evolved from classic (a dominatrix the first year, a vampire in 2005) to more complex (a skinless person in 2011) to complete cosplay. In 2015, Klum appeared as Jessica Rabbit; in 2018, as the ogre version of Fiona from Shrek. Last year, she was a Medusa, and her husband, Tom Kaulitz, a hoplite turned into stone. There are Hollywood-level prosthetics, and, largely, it appears as if her costumes are made more for an image than for a party. Klum, in this space, is both the trendsetter and the shining example of the way our collective take on the holiday has evolved to adjust to our online-first lifestyles.

“Someone I just started working with recently said, ‘We live in a reference economy,’” says stylist Ron Hartleben, who works with Camila Cabello and Tyla, among others. “That really struck me,” he says. “Everything has been done. Everyone has access to all the same images now.” So much so that people in the queer community “have gone about seeking the most niche, obscure reference from a show or pop culture moment and making that their Halloween costume” so that a mere mortal, in this case a cis, heterosexual person, may not understand it. “Gay Halloween is exploiting that obscure moment in pop culture and running with it to create one of the most stupid and entertaining outfits imaginable,” Hartleben says. “As long as you think it’s funny and you get it, you’re doing gay Halloween right.” Consider Benito Skinner and Mary Beth Barone’s costume this year as a shining example of gay Halloween: they dressed as Dakota Johnson and Ellen DeGeneres and even recreated their infamous, viral interview about the actor’s birthday party.

But gay Halloween has now broken past its own internet bubble. Celebrities and straight normies alike have adopted the reference-first language popular in queer and adjacent subcultures—from drag to ballroom and beyond—and made it mainstream to come off as more in-the-know.

Last year, Mandy Lee, a trend forecaster known as @oldloserinbrooklyn on TikTok and Instagram, dressed as Jonathan Anderson smoking a cigarette by the Seine, a video she reposted this year next to the original clip of Anderson to much online buzz (hers was taken by the Gowanus Canal in Brooklyn). “It’s a format that works particularly well online versus IRL because you’re able to [have] text onscreen or even throw up reference images to make it click,” Lee says. She categorizes her costumes as “fashion Halloween,” which she says lives under the same umbrella as gay Halloween. She’s dressed as Lynn Yaeger and Miuccia Prada before, and also the “tabi swiper.” The trick is that they are, as she says, “low effort.” They’re costumes that rely on what’s already in Lee’s closet—no production value, just a sense of humor. “It’s just fun to get hyper specific and granular,” Lee says. “[The costumes] are also not for everyone; they are for fashion people, and that’s what makes it fun.”

Earlier this week, stylist and creative director Chris Horan, who works with the likes of Charli xcx, Demi Lovato, and Christina Aguilera, reposted clips he’d been tagged in on Instagram of fans dressed as Adéla, for whom he is both stylist and creative director. “I obviously love when people dress up or reference any of the looks we’ve worked on,” Horan says. “It takes a lot of effort to make any sort of look on our part or [the fans’], so it always makes me happy to see it.”

Read Fit Check: Your front row seat to the power players, peacocks, and deep pockets of fashion—and how they influence the rest of the world.

Last year Horan worked with Lovato on her costume, for which she dressed as Poot Lovato, her fictional twin sister that originated from a Tumblr post in 2015. Poot had long been a gay Halloween staple, but her fans would have never imagined that Lovato herself would bring her back to the forefront in such a way. Horan thinks these costumes also speak to something bigger: “I don’t think you’re really hitting as a pop star if you don’t have an immediately identifiable look.”

The internet has changed the way we do most things, particularly getting dressed, so it’s no surprise that it would affect how we get dressed up. We do things not just for ourselves, or even the people who will see the costume IRL, but for our circles, or “followers,” to congratulate us. Social media may not have ruined Halloween—it’s made it funnier and perhaps less spooky—but it’s altered its spirit.

#3721. Yakuza Spiritual Successor Gang Of Dragon Seemingly Cancelled As Nagoshi Studio Is Closed

Gang of DragonToshihiro NagoshiYakuza: Like a Dragon

Toshihiro Nagoshi, the former general director of Like a Dragon maker Ryu Ga Gotoku Studio, formed Nagoshi Studio with some colleagues from his time at Sega a few years ago, and the studio’s first big game was going to be Gang of Dragon, a Yakuza spiritual successor that was first revealed at the 2025 Game Awards. However, after months of speculation surrounding the studio’s fate, an announcement in an official Japanese government gazette has revealed that Nagoshi Studio is no more.

The November 2nd edition of the government gazette, which reports official business closures and openings among other things, reported the finalized closure of the studio and its operations as of October 31st. The studio had been supported by NetEase Games as part of the latter’s expansive investment into Japanese gaming. In recent months, however, the news surrounding NetEaseâs various investments into Japanese studios has been defined by closures and cuts to funding. We now know this includes Nagoshi Studio.

Rumors surrounding the future of the company had been circulating heavily in recent months. Earlier this year, it was reported that the company was facing a shortfall in cash as NetEase pulled funding, with the studio needing roughly $44.4 million in order to finish development on its cinematic action title. Since then, there have been numerous signs that the company was being forced to wind down operations and cancel the project after being unable to acquire the needed funds elsewhereâthe social media accounts for the studio have not been updated since February, with the YouTube channel deleted and website becoming inaccessible in May before being restored.

Numerous talents have left the studio and joined other companies in recent months, so the writing was on the wall before the news was confirmed. Listings on places such as Steam still showÂ Gang of Dragon as coming soon, but itâs now very unlikely the title will see the light of day.

The fog of war clears around Embervale, revealing a survival crafting masterpiece.

PC Gamer's got your back Our experienced team dedicates many hours to every review, to really get to the heart of what matters most to you. Find out more about how we evaluate games and hardware.

What is it? A high-fantasy survival crafting RPG set in the genre's most impressive sandbox. Release date: October 15, 2026 (1.0) Expect to pay: $40/£35 Developer: Keen Games Publisher: Keen Games Reviewed on: RTX 4080, AMD Ryzen 7 9800X3D, 64GB RAM Steam Deck: Verified Link: Steam | Official site

High up on a mountain in the Albaneve Summits, just on the southern border of Enshrouded's new zone, I spot the perfect place for my next medieval building project. It seems safe with no nearby enemy spawns on the flat stretch of land, and there's even a cute frozen pond that gives it real Christmas-card appeal. I love it, and I'll love it even more once I've built a cliffside castle.

The only problem is I can't find a way up by climbing or gliding, so I'll have to make my own. I could build something, but that takes time, and I'm impatient. Instead, I behave like an absolute heathen—I bomb and pickaxe the hell out of the mountainside, carving a tunnel from the base to the top. It doesn't look great, but that's a problem for tomorrow's Flameborn.

That's always been one of my favorite parts of Enshrouded: you can destroy or build practically anything, anywhere in Embervale's voxel-based world. It's a survival crafting sandbox filled to the brim with handcrafted details, and every location still hidden by the fog of war could hold a new material, powerful weapon, or scenic vista. There's nothing quite like it, and just like the updates before, Enshrouded's 1.0 build keeps finding new, inventive ways to impress me long after I thought its well of surprises had run dry.

Enshrouded is a weird one. Not quite a traditional survival crafting game, but not a typical action RPG either. Its combat system and base building options are far more robust than most of its survival crafting cousins, but it's not nearly as brutal. I'm driven less by desperation and more by a desire to explore Embervale—a land devastated by a mysterious, malignant miasma known as (you guessed it) the Shroud. There's hardly a soul left in the world, so you learn more about its history from journals. Some are hastily scribbled by would-be heroes like you, while others are tragic retellings of someone's final days.

A few survivors remain as recruitable NPCs for your base. I love how lively they make player-made homes feel, even if the AI is a bit dopey.

One of my favorite additions in 1.0 is the voiceover added to every journal. The same narrator reads them all, giving the whole thing an endearing storybook feel as he shifts tone and pitch for different authors.

I found my favorite journal in a tiny, mountainside cave left by an old man grieving his wife. You can wander around the surrounding area for more environmental storytelling, but I have to warn you: some details got me teary-eyed.

So, for what must be the millionth time in my career, I stumble out of a mystical, sleepy haze confused and poorly dressed for the world I've awakened to. I am the Flameborn—a sort of ordained-by-god chosen one and the last hope for restoring the ruins of Embervale—but for now, I certainly don't feel that way. I just feel like some guy. It's a title I'll have to grow into, but will have to wait until I've upgraded from the aptly named 'ragged armor set'. Yeesh.

Enshrouded follows most of those rags-to-riches genre basics, so of course I'll graduate from an era of fighting with sticks and eating fistfuls of berries to magic-infused swords and Michelin-star meals. I've played so many of these games that the flow comes naturally now, but what I like most about Enshrouded's take on classic survival systems is that it drops the more punitive elements like fatigue, crafting chance, and even structural integrity.

Enshrouded has a robust set of custom difficulty options, but I learned the hard way to leave them alone until after you've tried the first dungeon.

An early access update added a custom setting for dehydration and starvation, but I much prefer playing without it .

There's cooking, farming, and even animal husbandry. Those systems are compelling enough as is, and don't gain anything by adding do-this-or-die mechanics.

Enshrouded knows that I, much like the family Golden Retriever, am treat-motivated. As long as there's shelter, fire, and decor, I'll get a stamina-boosting buff just by hanging out at home, but I'll never die from lack of sleep. In that regard, it's more like Valheim. Unique furnishings have their own comfort stats too, so there's incentive to explore Embervale for a new rug, fireplace, or even a toilet if you want a longer, more powerful boost. It's an especially exciting system for players like me, someone who loves building and decorating bases, but rarely sees a reward for the extra effort.

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

All this meticulous decorating makes me wonder whether I really want Enshrouded to add enemy raids on player bases and risk destroying them, but I'm leaning toward yes. It's the one major survival mechanic I miss in its formula, and I can't help but wistfully remember how fun it is to scramble into action when Valheim warns, "The forest is moving..." Imagine that, but with Enshrouded's poisonous fog instead.

Enshrouded has always been my favorite survival-crafting block set, but I'm thrilled with the new build camera. Building in tight corners is less hassle, and I don't slide off the roof a dozen times..

There's got to be a high fantasy Ikea hidden somewhere in Embervale, because the amount of furniture and decor in Enshrouded is absurd. It's nice to go from picking at scraps to being overwhelmed by choice

Version 1.0 also added Sparkworks, a logic system for creating your own enemy spawns, player-triggered events, special world builds, custom dungeons, and more. Your creations are shareable, too, so other players can suffer through your cruel obstacle course designs. I've tinkered with it myself, but I've mostly spent my time exploring player-made hobbit holes and feeling painfully self-conscious by comparison.

Repetitive tasks—another hunt for a rare material, another trek across the map—can become exasperating even in the best survival crafting games. There's a thin line between tedium and satisfaction, and Enshrouded walks it better than most. Much of that is thanks to the game's philosophy around punishment and reward, but its RPG elements add a layer of complexity that more than makes up for anything missing from Enshrouded's "survival-lite" approach.

Take my group, for example. I play with seven other friends, while that feels like a lot for most survival crafting games, Enshrouded's combat roles give us distinctly useful jobs. Rather than dumping points into three or four barebones stats, your Flameborn can specialize across 12 different skill trees. I mostly opt for tank, athlete, and assassin perks, but my allies fill other needs with mix-and-match builds for glass-cannon wizards, battlemage healers, or stealthy assassins. We also have our preferred responsibilities, like mining, woodcutting, gardening, cooking, and all those other usual genre chores.

Enshrouded's boss fights are a blast and more dynamic than similar games. Fights aren't as mechanically heavy as a Conan Exiles dungeon boss, but the traditional tank-and-spank approach won't cut it.

Hollow Halls—Enshrouded's massive dungeons that practically demand group play—are where combat roles shine the most. I beat one playing solo, but also wiped several times in a group of four.

A word of caution: multiplayer groups of more than two or three people should consider a dedicated server. Version 1.0 significantly improves performance, but not enough to spare bigger parties from the occasional murderous lag spike.

Multiplayer is also where some of my biggest gripes with Enshrouded remain, and despite heavy reworks to its questing systems, my group still struggled to make sense of the journal when our objectives fell out of sync. Our confusion mostly stemmed from completing world progression quests without the full party, so when absent friends logged back in, their to-do list didn't look the same and they had a list of missed quests. There are separate, personal quests to do at your own leisure, but we constantly compared our journals to make sure no one had gone off course.

I'm still not sure if any of that even mattered. No one was ever locked out of crafting recipes or new biomes because of the discrepancies, so the punishment boiled down to a smidge of missed XP and simply missing out on the moment. It didn't end up being a big deal, and I'm starting to think the journal's 'missed quest' label made the whole thing feel more consequential than it actually was. I clenched my jaw in frustration a few times, but if that's my biggest nitpick, then Enshrouded is survival crafting gold.

There's got to be a high fantasy Ikea hidden somewhere in Embervale, because the amount of furniture and decor in Enshrouded is absurd.

As much as I love the genre, I can't pretend it isn't filled with seemingly eternal early access pits. I've played in plenty of messy sandboxes, a handful of good ones, and just a few great ones. Then there's Enshrouded, operating in a league of its own. But even then, Enshrouded isn't just a good survival crafting game: it's a damn good game by any measure. Its building tools reward even my most impractical ambitions, and I'll never grow tired of exploring Embervale's hidden nooks and crannies.

Few games in the genre match its distinct identity or degree of polish, and after 500+ hours of adventuring, there's little left to wish for. My biggest dilemma post-Enshrouded will be moving on from a survival crafting RPG so lovingly handcrafted. I fear Keen Games has cooked up something that has forever changed my palate.

The fog of war clears around Embervale, revealing a survival crafting masterpiece.

Andrea has been covering games for nearly a decade, picking up bylines at IGN, USA Today, Fanbyte, and Destructoid before joining the PC Gamer team in 2025. She's got a soft spot for older RPGs and is willing to try just about anything with a lovey-dovey "I can fix them" romance element. Her weekly to-do always includes a bit of MMO time, endlessly achievement hunting and raiding in Final Fantasy 14. Outside of those staples, she's often got a few survival-crafting games on rotation and loves a good scare in co-op horror games.

#3719. What Happened to Detroit Lions’ Jack Campbell? Injury Explained

Detroit Lions linebacker Jack Campbell faced a scary on-field injury as the team faced off against the Minnesota Vikings.

Campbell was seemingly “immobilized” after a tackle against Vikings tight end T.J. Hockenson during the game at Detroit’s Ford Field on Sunday, November 1. (The Lions ultimately won 19-15 over the Vikings.)

The Lions’ athletic training staff swarmed Campbell, who did not appear to be able to move after the fall. He was then placed onto a backboard and transported to a local hospital.

“Heavy emotions in Detroit,” Michigan sportscaster Brad Galli wrote via X. “All the Lions players and coaches surrounded Jack Campbell before he was carted off at Ford Field.”

Campbell, an All-American college athlete during his time on the Iowa Hawkeyes, was selected by the Lions in the first round of the 2023 NFL Draft.

Scroll down to learn more about his injury:

The Lions shared in a statement on Sunday that Campbell was staying at the hospital overnight.

“Jack Campbell is resting and will remain in a local hospital tonight, for continued evaluation and monitoring,” the message shared via their official X account read. “The team will provide updates as we have them.”

In a postgame press conference, Lions head coach Dan Campbell shared that the linebacker was “being taken care of,” adding, “Thoughts and prayers are with Jack and his family.”

Lions quarterback Jared Goff shared that he was thinking about his teammate after the injury. “Jack’s deal was definitely scary,” Goff said on Sunday. “It just brings you back to reality for a moment that he’s a husband and a father. Scary. We’re praying for him and hope he’s going to be alright. If anyone is tough enough to get through something like that it’s going to be him.”

Tom Brady, who was calling the game on Fox, got candid about how the Lions could return to the field after the linebacker’s injury.

“It’s very difficult for everybody, obviously, but it’s also part of what you’ve been doing your whole life,” the former quarterback said. “He’s under great medical care and attention and you have to go back out there and do your job.”

Sideline commentator Erin Andrews also weighed in on Jack’s impact on the Lions organization while relaying a conversation with one of his teammates.

“He said, ‘This is Jack Campbell’s defense.’ I don’t hesitate to say that it goes through him and everyone in that locker room knows that,” Andrews said on Sunday. “Point blank period.”

Jack’s wife, Megan Campbell, has not spoken about his injury, but she was seen meeting him at field level on Sunday before he was taken to the hospital. The pair tied the knot in 2024 and welcomed their first baby, son Cooper, in July.

It’s been years since I’ve watched Steven Seagal’s only masterpiece, Under Siege. Luckily, the 1992 classic will be available with a Netflix subscription on November 6, and I plan on watching ASAP. It’s the one and only Seagal movie that is truly worth appointment viewing, and that’s for quite a few reasons, like the bonkers cast, the really cool shooting location, and, of course, Seagal at his physical peak (he’s a long way from that today). It should be, in my opinion, considered one of the best action movies of the 1990s.

You really have to kick this conversation off with the incredible cast of Under Siege. It’s rare that there are any other stars in a Seagal movie other than Seagal himself. That’s not true here. Instead of a faceless villain, we get Tommy Lee Jones as William Strannix, a former CIA operative with a serious case of narcissism. Jones is amazing in the role, as he so often is as a bad guy. The scene with Strannix eating roast beef with a chef's knife is peak ‘90s cinema. Usually, Seagal’s foes are two-dimensional, but not here.

Playing Strannix's sidekick is none other than Gary Busey. Sure, Busey doesn’t exactly have the best reputation in 2026, but in 1992, he was still thought of as a great actor, and he’s great here. He’s weaselly and slimy, and so easy to hate. He’s more hateable than Jones, that’s for sure. He’s actually perfect for the role at this point in his career. He’s a little crazy, but not too crazy, and it pays off on screen.

One of the movie's coolest aspects is its setting. At its heart, Under Siege is a heist movie, and Strannix and his band of thieves are targeting missiles on the USS Missouri, intended for the black market, hoping to spark World War III. In that respect, Strannix is basically a Bond villain trying to pull off an audacious crime to set in motion huge global changes. While shooting on the actual USS Missouri, one of the most decorated battleships in US Naval history, would have been tough to set up, they did shoot much of the movie on the USS Alabama, a retired World War II ship.

The Alabama and the Missouri are different class battleships, but they were both built just before or during the war, and are pretty similar. In a normal Seagal movie, you’d expect the whole thing to be filmed on a soundstage in Burbank, but not this one. They used a real ship, and it makes all the difference in how the movie looks. You really feel like you’re on the Missouri in this, and you believe that Seagal’s character, Casey Ryback, is a former Navy SEAL.

Seagal is really at the peak of his powers in Under Siege. He was coming off a wildly successful string of lower-budget action movies in the late ‘80s and early ‘90s, and he was ready for a big-time movie. In a lot of his later films (including Under Siege 2), he’s simply not believable as an unstoppable force, but he is in Under Siege, for sure. Though he’s been out of the spotlight for a long time, I do love going back to those early movies and remembering why Seagal was great and considered one of the biggest action stars of the ‘90s. Under Siege is the number one reason for that.

Hugh Scott is the Syndication Editor for CinemaBlend. Before CinemaBlend, he was the managing editor for Suggest.com and Gossipcop.com, covering celebrity news and debunking false gossip. #3717. Lenny Kravitz Was Not on Fatal Learjet Flight Despite Rumors, Rep Confirms

Lenny Kravitz is clearing up rumors that he was involved in a fatal plane crash in Florida over the weekend.

“The reports are untrue and incorrect,” Kravitz’s rep, Carleen Donovan, told BocaNewsNow.

On Sunday, November 1, a private jet bound for the Bahamas crashed in Palm Beach County, Florida, killing all nine people on board.

Rumors swirled on social media that Kravitz, 62, was among the passengers after a female pilot, who was wrongly identified as the person flying the doomed jet, posted about taking the singer on a similar route.

“Honored to be flying the one and only Lenny Kravitz from [Austin-Bergstrom International Airport] to [North Eleuthera Airport, Bahamas] tomorrow. Looking forward to having him on board,” read the since-deleted Facebook post from Florida-based pilot Emily Shelton.

Shelton also addressed the rumors that she was involved in the crash via TikTok on Sunday.

“I was recently made aware that there are rumors that I was the pilot of the recent crash in Palm Beach,” she wrote. “I would like to respectfully clarify I was not. I ask that people please stop speculating and spreading misinformation on this tragedy and be respectful of those involved. My heart goes out to all those lost and affected.”

The Learjet 60, which had taken off from Austin-Bergstrom International Airport in Texas, crashed into a roadway around 12:50 p.m. ET near Cresthaven and Greenacres, U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said in a statement.

“Today’s plane crash in Palm Beach County, Florida is a horrific tragedy,” Duffy wrote via X. “Please join me in praying for the families and loved ones of those we lost.”

No one on the ground was killed or injured, although flying debris from the fiery crash sparked localized fires and forced the emergency evacuation of approximately 600 mobile home residents, Palm Beach County District 3 Commissioner Joel Flores and Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis said.

Radio transmissions captured the crew reporting “light, clear ice that is manageable” and “moderate turbulence” while flying around 35,000 feet. The pilot then declared an emergency as the jet rapidly descended, stating over the radio, “We’re going to crash into the ground.”

DeSantis, 46, called the crash “cataclysmic.”

“It looked like a missile going down. It left a big crater on the side of the road,” he said.

Authorities have not yet released the identities of the nine victims, but one of the pilots was 20-year-old Nathalia Filgueiras, according to her mother.

The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) is investigating the incident with assistance from the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA).

#3716. Unpacking Nicki Minaj’s MAGA Style Evolution

This is the October 28, 2026 edition of Fit Check, your front row seat to the power players, peacocks, and deep pockets of fashion—and how they influence the rest of the world.

Pieter Mulier’s Versace debut will be marked with a couture show and the runway revival of Atelier Versace in January, and Bottega Veneta is back on Instagram for the first time since 2021—pouring one out to the fan accounts that had been enjoying their window of opportunity. Otherwise, the fashion news cycle has taken a break so far this week, so I’ve turned my attention to the midterm elections. Below, find missives on Nicki Minaj’s Gucci skirt suit by Demna—which was not provided to her by the brand—and the old style trick the Dems have adopted to appeal to us common folk. Plus, I get into why people love to clown Drake for his outfits. (For the record, I thought his Hermès by Martin Margiela fringed cape was fabulous.)

I wrote this edition of Fit Check wearing a sequined ghost costume (a ghost writer, get it?). It was my attempt at finding the right mindset to unpack what the internet has dubbed “gay Halloween,” for which I enlisted some of my fellow friends of Dorothy, and other experts, to help explain the formerly niche, now very viral internet phenomenon.

Mentioned in this issue: Jon Ossoff, Ralph Lauren, Bailey Moon, Juliet Charlotte, Marc Jacobs, Ariana Grande, Jonathan Anderson smoking a cigarette by the Seine, the breakup Post-it from a 2003 episode of Sex and the City, and many more.

“These Dem men with their hiked sleeves are taking me out,” read a comment under a clip of Senator Jon Ossoff and Pete Buttigieg on TikTok. “So hot.”

Ossoff and Buttigieg are the latest notable adopters of what appears to be the Democratic sartorial strategy for the ongoing midterm elections: to roll up their sleeves, literally. In a stark contrast to the most visible men on the right, who are all properly suited up both on the Hill in Washington, DC, and out on the campaign trail, “Dem men,” including Barack Obama and Gavin Newsom, have all been sporting a more casual look while campaigning. Individually, there’s nothing particular about the look. Obama and Buttigieg are former government officials; they’re technically off duty. Ossoff seems to want to position himself as a man of the people, and Newsom is working on embodying the anti-Trump. And yet, when seen together, the Dem men seem to have all agreed in a group chat to look a bit more working-class. No meticulously tailored Ralph Lauren suits, just dudes at work.

“There is a certain formula for cultivating a relaxed, approachable image while campaigning, versus the more polished presentation that comes with actually holding office,” says stylist Bailey Moon, who consulted with Dr. Jill Biden and Joe Biden during their time at the White House and worked with Tim Walz on the campaign trail in 2024. “It’s amusing to me, the idea that exposing your forearms suddenly makes you a man of the people, but rolling up your sleeves has become a political and metaphorical shorthand for being hardworking, accessible, and ready to get it done,” he says.

So is there a Dem men ’fit-pic group chat? “I don’t think there’s a coordinated effort,” Moon says. “I do think that politicians respond to a certain visual vocabulary, and right now, in a bid to win back working-class voters, that vocabulary is less formal and more familiar.”

Politicians do, in fact, think about their clothes more than we might think. “The visual language is always considered, even when the clothing itself isn’t front and center,” Moon says. “The challenge is making that feel instinctive rather than rehearsed, which ultimately comes down to the principal (key player) and how they carry it.” Ossoff et al. may not be folding up their sleeve cuffs as a joint campaign effort, and they may not be doing so to invoke some thirst in the comments section, but they’re making choices.

Drake celebrated his 40th birthday in New York City last weekend wearing black leather pants, a black turtleneck, and a brown fringed cape that got everyone talking. The rapper became the punch line of the weekend online before his outerwear piece was revealed as being a design by Martin Margiela during his time at Hermès—an archival holy grail find that Drake’s stylist, Juliet Charlotte, sourced from Canadian vintage seller Alex Maxamenko. He was called “Pumpkin Spice Papi,” a nod to his nickname and Instagram handle, @champagnepapi. He was compared to the Real Housewives venturing to Aspen on a girls trip. He was described as a rich auntie, and, my favorite, as ready for “Christian-girl autumn.”

The jokes were admittedly quite funny, and as we get into the “gay Halloween” phenomenon below, actor and comedian Sima Sepehri has already turned the viral moment into her costume. Yet underneath the surface of this mostly good-spirited fun—and my apologies for being the fun police—lies a layer of homophobia and, yes, misogyny. Drake has long been a punch line in the music industry and within hip-hop. People online have mocked him for the decor of his home and suggested he’d had a BBL or was showing off fake abs. He’s been called a wuss, and, pardon my French, a pussy. Which is where the issues with his style becoming a punch line begin.

Most of the jokes around Drake’s style compare him to women—to white women and their keenness for the fall season, to rich reality TV stars, to family matriarchs, and more. It’s simply too easy to call Drake and his penchant for fashion “feminine” or “fruity,” as if most famous men today, from his fellow rappers to athletes and actors, didn’t share his same affection for fashion and style. In a way, it’s not that serious. (And how he wore the shawl did look like he belonged more at a ski chalet than in the city.) Except that it kind of is; we have somehow not been able to shake gay as a zinger, and that’s generally because, culturally, we still consider femininity—and therefore women—to be less than masculinity and manliness. Let Drake wear his shawl. You’ve paid for it with your streams.

President Donald Trump and Nicki Minaj at a campaign event in Michigan.

President Trump made headlines last week for his comments on Senator Jon Husted’s physique, particularly his rear end. But he wasn’t done. This week, Trump attempted to crack a joke about it. “By the way, I looked at one hell of a beautiful ass before, Nicki Minaj,” the president said on Sunday at a Republican campaign rally in Michigan. “That’s hard to miss,” he said, before looking at the rapper and instructing her to “stand up!” Minaj did, and waved to the crowd and the president as if thanking him for the…uh, compliment.

Minaj has been a puzzling character to watch as she ventures deeper into the MAGA-sphere—she’s even been jokingly floated as a potential next White House press secretary. (Minaj held a mock interview about Trump aboard Air Force One, which was posted to X by White House communications director Steven Cheung with the caption, “Ladies and gentlemen, I think we may have found the new White House press secretary! @NICKIMINAJ.”)

On Sunday, the rapper was wearing a skirt suit by Gucci, retailing for about $4,000. Her look was finished with Pink Friday press-on nails, her own brand, and matching Gucci-logo pumps. In a way, the outfit is a departure from what one usually sees onstage at MAGA rallies, where luxury fashion—and particularly logos—rarely reign supreme unless coming from the first lady. Minaj, unlike other Trump acolytes, is often clad in on-trend designer clothes (when she joined President Trump at the Treasury Department Trump Accounts Summit in January of this year, she was wearing an Alaïa dress by Pieter Mulier), and while the idea of a prim skirt suit certainly suggested she was dressed for business, or at least for politics, the loud, allover monogram logo felt like a remnant of the musical superstar that was, or that remains somewhere underneath the surface.

As for what this means for Gucci, its clients likely won’t find the image of Minaj deterring—it’s not like the brand is underwriting Minaj’s appearance or the messaging around it. But perhaps the image of Minaj onstage will inspire the MAGA set to adopt Demna’s revamp of the house—some of the caricatural archetypes in his most recent collection certainly leaned conservative. Funnily enough, Karlie Kloss, wife of Josh Kushner and sister-in-law to Jared, wore a similar pencil skirt at Demna’s first Gucci runway show.

#3715. Zelda: Ocarina Of Time Remake Devs Tried Adding Even More Fast Travel Points, But That Sucked

The Legend of ZeldaThe Legend of Zelda: Ocarina Of Time

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake is out this week, and by all accounts we’ve heard so far, it seems like a pretty faithful remake, albeit with a lot of (necessary, in my opinion) technical and mechanical smoothing out from the original. I don’t envy the devs working on this one (which we now know to be Nintendo EPD): Ocarina of Time is a classic that everyone has really, really strong feelings about. Deciding what to change and what not to change must have been a huge headache.

Which is why I’m so, so glad that Eiji Aonuma backtracked on his own ridiculous idea to add a bunch of new fast-travel pointsÂ to this game.

This came up during an Ask the Developer interview published by Nintendo today. Now, the original Ocarina of Time already has some fast travel, in that Link can eventually learn ocarina songs that will warp him to each of five of the game’s major dungeons, plus the Temple of Time. And honestly, that’s quite enough to be getting on with, thanks. One of these songs is actually necessary to even access its associated dungeon in the first place, as you need child Link at the Desert Colossus, but he can’t get into Gerudo Valley without being adult Link and riding Epona.

But at one point in the remake’s development, longtime Zelda producer and franchise steward Eiji Aonuma thought this wasn’t enough. As Aonuma explains, he observed that a lot of players tried to move around the world faster in the original by spamming Link’s dodge roll, which led him to think there may need to be a faster way to get around the world.

I thought we needed to address this in this new version. So I asked the team to add warp points that didnât exist in the original game, giving players access to shortcuts. But when we actually tried playing the game with those warp points, we realized that we were missing out on the moments of discovery that came from stopping along the way and wondering, âWait, whatâs this?â Through this development process, we were reminded once again just how important those moments are to the very structure of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time. So even though I was the one who proposed adding warp points, they just weren’t working for me in the end, so I got the team to take them all back out again. (Laughs)

Honestly, what a relief. He’s spot on, really. I played Ocarina of Time for the first time back in January, and while there were times when I was grateful to have a quick way to get from, say, Zora’s Domain all the way back to Castle Town without hoofing it through multiple loading zones I’ve seen a dozen times before, a lot of my favorite discoveries in this game came from being forced to hike around and trip over interesting things. There are all sorts of hidden bits in Hyruleâheart pieces, rupees, goofy little characters.

I also just don’t know where you’d even put more fast travel points. I guess I can imagine Aonuma wanting to add warp points to places like Kokiri Forest, Lon Lon Ranch, Zora’s Domain, and other major spots. But if you did that, then why would you ever need to even be in Hyrule Field? Ocarina of Time is not a massive game! It does not take that long to cross Hyrule Field, especially on Epona! It’s pretty easy to get to all those spots from the temple warps! Kids these days don’t want to go on long walks through grassy, Peahat-ridden plains anymore!

Mostly I just think it’s funny that Aonuma both proposed this idea and ultimately rejected it. Elsewhere in the interview, Aonuma talks about how the development of this remake involved handing off this old classic to individuals who had never played it until they were put on the project and letting them make their own decisions about how much to alter:

If the producers say, âThis is how it should be,â the team would naturally feel obligated to do it that way. So I basically let the developers make whatever changes they genuinely felt were necessary. I wanted the team to make The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time their own, and to follow through on their own ideas about what the game should be. That said, I did deliver my fair share of lectures along the way. (Laughs) I took a step back to observe how the younger members of the development team would reimagine The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time using the insights and answers they had arrived at on their own.

The remake of Ocarina of Time is out later this week, on November 5, and a second part of this Ask the Developer interview is dropping tomorrow. You should read the entirety of it when you get the chance, as it’s pretty neat, though it’s left me desperately wanting to hear whatever “bright and upbeat” piece of music Kondo originally composed for Ganondorf’s theme way back in the ’90s.

I tried the demo for Queen's Domain last year and liked it a lot⁠—though it definitely had some friction I wasn't sure about. The full game launched on October 30, and I eagerly rushed through the parts I'd already played in the demo.

Turns out, that demo cut out right when things were about to go nuts.

Five hours in out of an estimated 30+, and Queen's Domain is easily one of my top games of the year. I am only begrudgingly writing this, because I'd rather be playing right now.

Queen's Domain starts out resembling other entries in a growing subgenre of indie King's Field-likes, paying homage to the first-person dark fantasy RPG series FromSoftware put out before its soulsward turn. In its first half hour or so, Queen's Domain distinguishes itself similarly to fellow genre standout Lunacid: Fantastic art, maybe even better music, and a mastery of nostalgic intangibles (menu, UI, sound cues, etc.) After beating the first boss, Queen's Domain rewards you with a magic airdash sword, and it's at that point that the game truly begins.

Queen's Domain is a very deliberately paced game and, like a lot of first-person RPGs, it starts out feeling like your boots will always be on the ground. Think the difference between Doom and Quake: You can mostly tell when a game will let you get some air or not.

But once I was rocking the Holy Sword, Endu? Holy shit. Queen's Domain's first area opens up like some wonderful clockwork contraption. A lot of the verticality reminds me of Destiny raids, the way hidden paths blend into the environment, and reaching them feels like you're sequence breaking.

Endu can be upgraded with special gems throughout the game, with each giving you an extra dash while airborne. I'm up to three at the time of writing, and each upgrade has felt like it radically opened up my traversal options: There are parts of the first few maps I'm pretty sure I'll only be able to reach once I'm up to four or five dashes, zooming from one end of the map to the other without touching the ground.

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

Endu's a standout, but it's not the only tool available: Queen's Domain seems to have an expansive arsenal, and weapons can transform as they're upgraded. You upgrade weapons just by using them, and the game has no stat allocation on level up, encouraging experimentation with the arsenal⁠—PC Gamer hardware writer James Bentley managed to max upgrade 20 weapons across his full playthrough. You can effectively create a "build" via your choice of which weapons to hotkey (limit of three) and upgrade, a system that more resembles BioShock or the System Shock Remake rather than something like Dark Souls or Lunacid.

My favorite alongside Endu so far has been the Caestus, a type of medieval knuckle duster that's been a standby of the Souls games. Here, it's a fast-attacking blunt weapon useful against slashing-resistant skeletons. Instead of a horizontal dash like Endu, its special attack is an uppercut that launches my character into the air. Plenty of fun to use on enemies, but I've loved deploying it as an effective double jump to reach otherwise-inaccessible areas⁠—and there's always been a surprise or meaningful reward waiting for me when I do.

My coworker, PCG staff writer Morgan Park, initially bounced off the pre-Endu, demo-equivalent portion of Queen's Domain. I'm here to say stay strong, prayer warriors. It is worth getting through that first half hour. While there's something to be said about it potentially putting new players off, I think the contrast between pre-and post-Endu gameplay is so strong, it makes the air dash feel all the more powerful. You know what it's like to be stuck on the ground, and you won't take it for granted.

It's the sort of contrast metroidvanias thrive on⁠—I always think of how dinky you feel before you get the wall jump in Hollow Knight⁠—and Queen's Domain's brilliant level design might leave it the best first-person metroidvania anyone's made since the first Metroid Prime.

And I think Prime's a strong comparison point overall here: The cryptic atmosphere, breathtaking vistas, and genuinely unique approach to first-person movement and level design speak to that. I'm already seeing hints toward game-spanning backtracking in my future, but I've got reason to suspect Queen's Domain's backtracking will be less frustrating and obtuse than Metroid Prime's.

I already love this game, and I am about to mainline it over the next 30 hours or so of my free time⁠—stay tuned for our full Queen's Domain review to come. Meanwhile, Queen's Domain is available on Steam for a launch price of $17, down from an MSRP of $20.

He is obsessed with all things CRPG and CRPG-adjacent, but has also covered esports, modding, and rare game collecting. #3713. 'Criminal Minds' EP Breaks Silence After Shocking Cancellation

Criminal Minds‘ sudden ending seemingly came as a surprise to those working behind the scenes.

“It’s hard to put into words what Criminal Minds has meant to all of us who have been fortunate enough to be part of this extraordinary journey, first on CBS for 15 seasons and then on Paramount+ for five,” showrunner and executive producer Erica Messer said while breaking her silence on the shocking development.

Messer hinted the writers didn’t go into season 20 thinking it would be their last.

“While suddenly navigating the end of this chapter, I’m filled with gratitude for our remarkable cast, writers, directors and crew who have poured their hearts into this show, and for the incredible fans around the world whose unwavering loyalty has kept Criminal Minds going for two decades,” she continued. “We’re looking forward to sharing season 20 with everyone, and celebrating the legacy of this special show we’ve all built together.”

Criminal Minds originally premiered in 2005, following a group of criminal profilers who work for the FBI as members of its Behavioral Analysis Unit. The series was revived by Paramount+ as Criminal Minds: Evolution after its initial conclusion in 2020.

Many of the original stars returned for Evolution, with Joe Mantegna, A.J. Cook, Vangsness, Aisha Tyler, Adam Rodriguez and Paget Brewster reprising their roles. Other key characters — such as Matthew Gray Gubler‘s Reid — have also made appearances.

Following the show’s shocking ending, several Criminal Minds cast members have spoken out.

“This has happened. It’s being canceled. Then it says right there, it’s ending for now,” Vangsness, 54, who has played Penelope Garcia throughout the show’s 20 seasons, said in an Instagram video on Friday, October 30.

“You know that part in Charlie and the Chocolate Factory where Charlie gets the chocolate and it’s like a little bittersweet, because he’s like, ‘Thanks so much for the chocolate,’” the actress explained. “Look how long, that doesn’t happen ever. But I love my job and my boss Erica Messer says there’s so many more stories to tell. So, if we get to keep telling them somewhere, that would be amazing.”

She continued: “I know all of us feel the same way. … Everything’s OK. Aren’t we all in a death and rebirth cycle? Yes, so maybe this goes somewhere else? What an adventure.”

Criminal Minds season 20 is expected to premiere in 2027.

Celebrities brought their A-game this Halloween. From Megan Fox going full Twilight as a gothic vampire to Carmen Electra dressing as Catwoman, A-listers truly sought to lean on creativity and individuality when devising their looks for the holiday. As for Jennifer Lopez, she decided to go for a topless look to channel her Monster-In-Law co-star, Jane Fonda, while dressing as the powerful Barbarella.

Jennifer Lopez has proved time and again this year what a fashionista she is. Most recently, she looked dreamy and romantic at Paris Fashion Week wearing a sheer dress and brought fall vibes in a fur coat and sheer, luxe black dress. For Halloween, you couldn’t expect anything less, as her Barberella look was not only fierce but also served as a fitting tribute to one of Jane Fonda's most distinct movie roles. Check it out in the Instagram post below:

For those who don’t know, Barbarella is a campy cult classic that sees Fonda portraying a futuristic female astronaut who encounters strange planets while trying to locate Dr. Durand-Durand. One of the Roger Vadim-directed sci-fi flick’s most memorable qualities is the array of outlandish futuristic costumes that Fonda wears. With that in mind, Lopez couldn’t have picked a better movie to channel for her Halloween costume this year.

The Maid in Manhattan actress is showing the right to bear arms while wearing Barbarella’s mesh silver-laced dress with metallic boots. I’m also loving the white bodysuit with the black vertical stripes running down. The ‘60s blonde wig she’s wearing as the aforementioned character is such a nice nod to the decade and fictional space heroines in general.

And Lopez can’t celebrate the cult classic’s sexual liberation theme without taking a topless photo of herself, which sees her posing with blind angel Pylar. All in all, JLo looks like she’s having a lot of fun honoring her former co-star’s psychedelic movie.

With how on-point Jennifer Lopez looks as Barbarella, you’d think she was auditioning for the remake of the 1968 film. I mean, she’s wearing each outfit with such pizzazz and poise. However, Sydney Sweeney is set to “save the universe” as the film's lead. The actress seems like a great fit, and I'm confident she'll do a great job embodying the iconic space adventurer.

Per what's known about the remake, Edgar Wright has been in talks to direct, while Kingsman's Jane Goldman and Honey Ross have also been approached to write the screenplay. While the upcoming science-fiction movie is still in its development stages, it’s great that the “On the Floor” singer is already bringing the movie back into the general public's consciousness.

When it comes to the long line of costumes Jennifer Lopez has worn for Halloween over the years, these Barbarella looks may be amongst my favorites. If anything, now I'd like to know how Jane Fonda feels about her former co-star paying tribute to her and her character. In the meantime, anyone who's curious and wants to check out Barbarella can do so by watching the movie for free on Pluto TV.

Just your average South Floridian cinephile who believes the pen is mightier than the sword.

#3711. New Port Of NFS Underground 2 Turns The Beloved PS2 Racer Into A Wild MMO

It’s a day ending in the letter “Y,” so you know what that means? Yup, another classic video game has been ported in some oddball way with the assistance of AI coding. This time around, someone has gotten PlayStation 2 classic Need for Speed: Underground 2 playable via a web browser, and in this version, you can race alongside dozens of other people at the same time.

Need for Speed: Underground 2 was released back in 2004 and became one of the most popular games of the year thanks to its open-world design and Fast and Furious-like nighttime racing action. It’s like a proto-Forza Horizon, but with a lot more underglow and NOS. And now, thanks to NFS Underground 2 Revived, if you have nostalgic memories of Underground 2 and want to once again drift around its city streets, you can do so in your web browser without having to download a single file or install anything. Oh, and if you want, you can now relive your nostalgia alongside some of the thousands of players currently enjoying this Underground 2 port, according to the site’s data. Just be prepared for some chaos.

My favorite childhood racing game got imported to a website and now 3000 people are free roaming.. this is so fucking funny pic.twitter.com/cUCiz6JDRm

NFSU2 Revived was released late last month, but has recently blown up as fans have discovered the free-to-play browser port via viral clips of the dozens of player-controlled cars smashing into each other on streets that were never designed for this kind of online multiplayer mayhem.Â  Don’t worry, you don’t have to race with others if you just want to enjoy the original solo experience of NSFU2 on your PC in 2026. The multiplayer chaos is opt-in.

The person behind this port claims that they used to play Underground 2 when they were younger, and the creator put this project together so they could “play together again.”

“It worked surprisingly well, and it got a bit out of hand,” said the fan modder and developer. “It’s great to see so many people playing it.”

And as mentioned up top, yes, this port was developed with the help of AI tools, as documented on the Revived’s GitHub page. While I’m not a fan of the AI enshittifcation of the world, it’s also getting harder and harder to play or report on cool game projects and retro mods, like Revived, without running into some amount of AI coding. I’ve talked to numerous devs, big and small, working on these kinds of projects, and for many, these tools are just part of their workflow now.

Now we wait to see if EA, the original publisher of Underground 2, steps in and shuts this all down. Though the company does seem a bit busy right now…

#3710. Vikings’ T.J. Hockenson Reacts to Lions Linebacker Jack Campbell’s Injury

Minnesota Vikings tight end T.J. Hockenson is sharing a message of support for Detroit Lions linebacker Jack Campbell after an on-field injury.

“I said this earlier, but prayers out to Jack Campbell, man, and his family,” Hockenson, 29, told reporters after the Sunday, November 1, game. “I was in on that play. I didn’t see what happened, but that’s an Iowa guy. I know Jack, and I just want to send good vibes to him and his family and his locker room.”

He continued, “We’re competitors, but at the end of the day, we’re on the same team. We put our body on the line every Sunday. So, just good vibes and prayers over to that guy.”

Campbell, 26, went down during the Sunday game at Detroit’s Ford Field after a tackle against Hockenson. He was transported to a local hospital, where he stayed overnight. Campbell’s wife, Meghan, was seen joining him on the field and traveling with him to the hospital via an ambulance.

“Like I said, we do this every single Sunday. We go out there. We know what we signed up for. But you never want to see that,” Hockenson said on Sunday. “You never want to see anyone go down at the end of the day. You don’t ever want to see that. Get down on a knee, say a prayer and hope for the best. God’s got him in his hands. He’s got a plan for him.”

He continued, “You just gotta keep playing unfortunately, and you gotta get back in the mindset of the game goes on. But obviously for him, his family, I know how much that impacts. I’ve been injured. … A lot of prayers and a lot of good vibes from this locker room over to him.”

The Lions ultimately were victorious over the Vikings 19-15. In a post-game press conference, Lions quarterback Jared Goff offered his support to Campbell — who is a father — and his family. (Campbell tied the knot with Megan in 2024, and the pair welcomed their son one year later.)

“Jack’s deal was definitely scary,” Goff, 32, said after the Sunday game. “It just brings you back to reality for a moment that he’s a husband and a father. Scary. We’re praying for him and hope he’s going to be all right. If anyone is tough enough to get through something like that, it’s going to be him.”

Nathan Fielder's You Can See Everything has been stirring up buzz and earning its fair share of money. However, one honor that had been alluding it was the No. 1 spot at the box office. Well, that's no longer the case, as the doc finally became the top movie in the United States this weekend. And regardless of whether that win can be attributed to people showing up because of all the Oscar buzz, or the scene that literally shows everything, it's also resulted in the documentary obtaining a very rare honor.

It should be mentioned that Fielder's film just barely won the top spot, as Warner Bros. and DC Studios' Clayface just missed winning Halloween weekend after its strong start by a little less than $200,000. Wildwood, which some are calling one of the best and scariest movies of the year, remains in third place this week, while steamy fantasy flick Wicker climbed another spot too. Check out the full breakdown below:

6. BTS World Tour ‘Arirang’ in Buenos Aires and São Paulo Live Viewing

9. The Only Living Pickpocket In New York

The No. 1 spot aside, this is a truly auspicious moment for You Can See Everything, because in a rare turn of events, it's now the fourth documentary ever to win a weekend box office. With that, it now joins Fahrenheit 9/11, Michael Jackson's This Is It and Taylor Swift: The Official Release Of A Showgirl. That's a lineup even more wtf than some of the moments in the film. Nevertheless, this is quite the distinction for Fielder and co.

I Wondered Why Nathan Fielder Was Picked For You Can See Everything. His Answer Confused Me

One way YCSE differentiates itself from this lineup, however, is by having a different path to this milestone. All three of the other movies managed to win the box office in their opening weekends. You Can See Everything opened at No. 2 at the box office weeks ago and held that spot last week before finally grabbing the top spot this week.

Whether Fielder's film will hold that spot again next week remains to be seen. Clayface is still sticking around, and it had about 200 more theaters screening the body horror thriller this weekend. That comic book film is already proving to be a solid win for DC, as it has grossed roughly $83 million worldwide against a reported budget between $30 and $44 million.

Plus, a new month means a new slate of films arriving on the 2026 movie schedule. The Cat in the Hat and Godzilla Minus Zero are among the titles arriving in a week's time, and there's always the chance that they could shake things up at the B.O. next week.

All this to say, I expect You Can See Everything to stick around the Top 10 for at least a few more weeks based on how it's trending. I'm very curious as to just how much longer it'll continue to haul in millions, as I don't know if anyone saw this run coming. I'm just hoping to hear that this means Nathan Fielder is going to get more documentaries in theaters, which I would absolutely love to see.

#3708. Overwatch’s Director Explains Why The Same Few Heroes Keep Getting Skins

The distribution of cosmetic skinsâwhich heroes get the lionâs share and which ones get significantly fewerâ is a pretty sensitive subject in the Overwatch community. Years of Mercy, Kiriko, and Juno players constantly eating good while Baptiste, Venture, and Wrecking Ball players wait months if not years for a new Legendary skin have some people jaded about the whole process, with some players even criticizing some of the gameâs base hero designs as feeling like they are made with a âcosmetics-firstâ mindset.

During a group interview Kotaku was present for, game director Aaron Keller talked about the challenges of giving attention to its soon-to-be 55 heroes in not just cosmetics, but in storylines the game has introduced over the gameâs 10 years. He says itâs a problem the team at Blizzard has been dealing with for years, one which he admits is âtrickyâ as the roster grows.

âEvery new piece of content that we introduce to the game, whether it’s a hero or even a map, you know, means that the pool of everything that we’ve got, it is spread out a little bit,â he says. âWe recognize how important it is to continue supporting all of the different heroes in the game. And on one side of it, it’s cosmetics, but as we delve into the story and the narrative for the game, you hear from a lot of players about like, âHey, when is this particular hero going to enter the story?â Or, âIt felt like you kind of left off, let’s say, for example, the story of Zarya years ago. When are you going to pick that thing back up?â And so it definitely makes that more difficult.â

With the introduction of the battle pass and frequent store refreshes, Overwatch is producing more skins in recent years than it used to when the game was primarily supported through loot boxes. Keller says that while the team has to prioritize characters who âsupport the actual bottom-line business,â he hopes that initiatives like creating two customizable Mythic skins per season can allow them to more frequently support heroes that have gotten less love over the years, while also always featuring at least one who typically drives skin sales.

âAs a team we have been, over the past few years, constantly expanding our capacity and our throughput for the amount of skins that we make. And as we do that, it allows us to not just make skins for a lot of the heroes that, if I’m being honest, do more to support the actual bottom-line business for the game,â Keller says. âAnd it also allows us to start making cosmetics for some of our other heroes. The place that you can see that the most transparently is the Mythic skins that we release. Each season we release two Mythic skins, and typically one of those is going to be for a hero that we think is actually going to really drive a lot of that support for the business. And then another one is going to be for a hero that typically hasn’t gotten either a Mythic or a lot of other skins in the recent past. So we recognize it’s important to players. We want to be doing as much of it as we can, but we still always want to be doing it in a way that’s also responsible, and [lets us] know that we can continue supporting this game going forward.â

Overwatch started putting out two Mythic skins per season a year ago in October of 2025, and Iâd say most of the seasons that have followed have adhered to the blueprint Keller describes, featuring one hero who is a tried-and-true seller of skins and another one whoâs gotten less love over the years. Lifeweaver and Junkrat are a good example of a pair of heroes who are on opposite ends of the skin-receiving spectrum, but you also have last season when Genji and Widowmaker both got their second Mythic skins in the same batch, a move which frustrated many players who were waiting for an underserved hero to get the spotlight. The current season, which began on October 6, launched with a Mythic skin for Wuyang, who has received several skins since his launch last year. Weâll see what the second Mythic is when the gameâs midseason phase begins later this week.
